docs.title: Worked Examples
docs.text:
Example 10 — Comparing Bond Strength Signatures

Rank covalent, ionic, and metallic bonds by which is most likely to produce a brittle solid versus a malleable one, and explain why.

Solution: Covalent and ionic bonds are both directional or fixed in their electrostatic geometry; when stressed enough to shift atoms out of position, these bonds break outright rather than reforming, producing brittleness (characteristic of both silicon/diamond and NaCl). Metallic bonds have no fixed directionality — the electron sea simply redistributes as ion cores slide past one another — so metals are typically malleable rather than brittle.

Example 11 — Predicting Bond Type from Valence Electrons

An element has 6 valence electrons and high electronegativity. Predict whether it is more likely to form covalent, ionic, or metallic bonds with a low-electronegativity metal partner, and explain why.

Solution: With 6 valence electrons, this element needs only 2 more to complete an octet, and its high electronegativity means it strongly attracts additional electrons rather than donating its own. Paired with a low-electronegativity metal (which readily gives up electrons), the most likely outcome is an ionic bond, with the metal donating electrons and this element accepting them to complete its octet — the same logic that produces NaCl from sodium and chlorine.

Example 12 — Total Shared Electrons in a Silicon Crystal Fragment

A small fragment of a silicon crystal contains 6 interior silicon atoms, each fully bonded to 4 neighbors within the fragment. How many covalent bonds, and how many total shared electrons, does this fragment contain? (Assume every bond is fully contained within the fragment, so no bonds are double-counted at the boundary.)

Solution: Each of the 6 atoms forms 4 bonds, giving \(6\times4=24\) bond-ends; since each bond has two ends (one at each atom it connects), the number of distinct bonds is \(24/2=12\). Each bond shares 2 electrons, so the total number of shared electrons is \(12\times2=24\).

docs.title: Chapter 4 Glossary
docs.text: Terms introduced in Chapter 4 — Chemical Bonding in Semiconductor Crystals. See the full site Glossary for terms across all chapters.

docs.title: Amorphous Solid
docs.text:
A solid in which atoms preserve roughly the same local bonding environment a crystal would prefer, but with no long-range periodic order extending beyond a few atomic spacings.

Example: Amorphous silicon (a-Si) preserves silicon's approximate 4-fold local coordination but lacks the long-range periodicity of single-crystal silicon, and is used in low-cost thin-film solar cells.

See also: Polycrystalline Solid, Crystal Lattice.

Contrast with: Polycrystalline Solid, which retains long-range order within each grain, and a single crystal, which retains it throughout.

docs.title: Covalent Bond
docs.text:
A chemical bond formed when two atoms each contribute one valence electron to a shared electron pair that is electrostatically attracted to both nuclei; directional, and the bond type used by silicon and germanium.

Example: Each silicon atom forms 4 covalent bonds, one to each of 4 tetrahedrally-arranged neighbors, satisfying its octet by counting the 8 total electrons shared across those 4 bonds.

See also: Valence Electron, Tetrahedral Bonding.

Contrast with: Ionic Bond, which transfers electrons completely rather than sharing them, and Metallic Bond, which delocalizes electrons across the entire crystal.

docs.title: Crystal Defect
docs.text:
Any local disruption of the ideal, perfectly periodic crystal lattice, including point defects such as vacancies (missing atoms), interstitials (extra atoms between regular sites), and substitutional impurities (foreign atoms replacing host atoms).

Example: A phosphorus atom occupying a silicon lattice site is a substitutional defect — the same mechanism deliberately exploited during doping in Chapter 8.

See also: Amorphous Solid, Polycrystalline Solid.

docs.title: Electronegativity
docs.text:
A measure of how strongly an atom's nucleus attracts electrons in a chemical bond, used together with valence electron count to predict whether a bond will be covalent, ionic, or metallic.

Example: Chlorine's high electronegativity and sodium's low electronegativity together favor complete electron transfer, producing the ionic bond in NaCl.

See also: Valence Electron, Ionic Bond.

docs.title: Grain Boundary
docs.text:
The thin, disordered boundary region separating two differently-oriented single-crystal grains within a polycrystalline solid.

Example: In polycrystalline silicon ("polysilicon"), grain boundaries scatter charge carriers and degrade electronic performance relative to single-crystal silicon.

See also: Polycrystalline Solid.

docs.title: Ionic Bond
docs.text:
A chemical bond formed when one atom transfers one or more valence electrons completely to another, producing oppositely charged ions held together by Coulomb attraction; non-directional.

Example: Sodium transfers its single valence electron to chlorine, forming \(\text{Na}^+\) and \(\text{Cl}^-\) ions bound by \(U(r) = -e^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0 r)\).

See also: Valence Electron, Electronegativity.

Contrast with: Covalent Bond, which shares electrons rather than transferring them.

docs.title: Metallic Bond
docs.text:
A chemical bond in which the valence electrons of every atom in a crystal delocalize into a shared, mobile "electron sea" surrounding fixed positive ion cores; non-directional and responsible for metals' electrical conductivity and malleability.

Example: Copper's single, loosely-bound valence electron delocalizes readily, producing an electron sea that explains copper's high conductivity and malleability.

See also: Valence Electron.

Contrast with: Covalent Bond and Ionic Bond, in which electrons remain localized to a specific bond or ion rather than delocalizing across the whole crystal.

docs.title: Polycrystalline Solid
docs.text:
A solid composed of many small single-crystal regions, called grains, each internally periodic but oriented at a different angle relative to its neighbors, separated by grain boundaries.

Example: Polycrystalline silicon ("polysilicon") is widely used for gate electrodes and interconnects in integrated-circuit fabrication.

See also: Grain Boundary, Amorphous Solid.

Contrast with: Amorphous Solid, which lacks long-range order even within small regions, and a single crystal, which has no grain boundaries at all.

docs.title: Silicon Atom Structure
docs.text:
The electron configuration of a neutral silicon atom (atomic number 14), \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^2\), consisting of 10 chemically inert core electrons and 4 valence electrons.

Example: Silicon's group-14 position in the periodic table directly reflects its 4 valence electrons, the same count germanium (also group 14) shares.

See also: Valence Electron.

docs.title: sp3 Hybridization
docs.text:
The quantum-mechanical combination of one \(s\) orbital and three \(p\) orbitals into four new, equivalent hybrid orbitals that point toward the corners of a regular tetrahedron.

Example: Silicon's \(3s\) and three \(3p\) valence orbitals hybridize into 4 sp3 orbitals, each forming one covalent bond, producing the tetrahedral bond angle of \(109.5°\).

See also: Tetrahedral Bonding, Valence Electron.

docs.title: Tetrahedral Bonding
docs.text:
The bonding geometry in which an atom's four covalent bonds point toward the corners of a regular tetrahedron, at a bond angle of \(109.5°\), produced by sp3 hybridization.

Example: Silicon's tetrahedral bonding directly produces the diamond lattice structure's coordination number of 4, introduced geometrically in Chapter 3.

See also: sp3 Hybridization, Diamond Lattice Structure.

docs.title: Valence Electron
docs.text:
An electron in an atom's outermost occupied shell, available for participation in chemical bonding; the count and behavior of these electrons determines which bonding type an atom prefers.

Example: Silicon has 4 valence electrons (from \(3s^2\,3p^2\)), the single number that determines its preference for covalent, tetrahedral bonding.

See also: Silicon Atom Structure, Covalent Bond.

docs.title: Chapter 4 Problems - Chemical Bonding in Semiconductor Crystals
End-of-Chapter Problems: Chemical Bonding in Semiconductor Crystals
docs.text: Work through these problems to reinforce your understanding of the chemical bonding covered in Chapter 4.

docs.title: Problem 1
docs.text:
State silicon's full electron configuration.

Show Solution

\(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^2\).

docs.title: Problem 2
docs.text:
How many valence electrons does a neutral silicon atom have, and which subshells do they occupy?

Show Solution

4 valence electrons, occupying the \(3s^2\,3p^2\) subshells.

docs.title: Problem 3
docs.text:
Define, in one sentence, a covalent bond.

Show Solution

A covalent bond forms when two atoms each contribute one valence electron to a shared electron pair that is electrostatically attracted to both nuclei.

docs.title: Problem 4
docs.text:
Define, in one sentence, an ionic bond.

Show Solution

An ionic bond forms when one atom transfers one or more valence electrons completely to another, producing oppositely charged ions held together by Coulomb attraction.

docs.title: Problem 5
docs.text:
Define, in one sentence, a metallic bond.

Show Solution

A metallic bond forms when the valence electrons of every atom in a crystal delocalize into a shared, mobile electron sea surrounding fixed positive ion cores.

docs.title: Problem 6
docs.text:
State the tetrahedral bond angle produced by sp3 hybridization.

Show Solution

\(109.5°\).

docs.title: Problem 7
docs.text:
Define, in one sentence, an amorphous solid.

Show Solution

An amorphous solid preserves roughly the same local atomic bonding a crystal would prefer, but has no long-range periodic order beyond a few atomic spacings.

docs.title: Problem 8
docs.text:
Name the three basic types of point crystal defects.

Show Solution

Vacancy (a missing atom), interstitial (an extra atom between regular sites), and substitutional (a foreign atom replacing a host atom).

docs.title: Problem 9
docs.text:
Show explicitly why a silicon atom forming 4 covalent bonds satisfies the octet rule, even though silicon itself supplies only 4 electrons.

Show Solution

Each of silicon's 4 bonds is a shared pair containing 2 electrons: 1 from silicon and 1 from the neighboring atom. Silicon counts both electrons of every bond it participates in toward its own octet, so \(4\text{ bonds}\times2\text{ electrons/bond}=8\) electrons in its local environment, even though silicon's own contribution was only 4.

docs.title: Problem 10
docs.text:
Estimate the Coulomb potential energy, in electron-volts, between two ions of opposite unit charge separated by \(r=0.31\) nm.

Show Solution

\(U(r) = -\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(1.602\times10^{-19})^2}{0.31\times10^{-9}} = -7.45\times10^{-19}\ \text{J} \approx -4.6\ \text{eV}\).

docs.title: Problem 11
docs.text:
Explain why sodium tends to bond metallically with other sodium atoms, but ionically when paired with chlorine.

Show Solution

Among identical sodium atoms, there is no electronegativity difference to drive complete electron transfer, so each atom's loosely-bound single valence electron simply delocalizes into a shared electron sea, favoring a metallic bond. Paired with highly electronegative chlorine, however, sodium's single valence electron transfers completely to chlorine's outer shell, favoring an ionic bond instead.

docs.title: Problem 12
docs.text:
Show explicitly how silicon's 1 valence \(3s\) orbital and 3 valence \(3p\) orbitals combine into sp3 hybrid orbitals, and state how many bonds this allows silicon to form.

Show Solution

Hybridization conserves the total orbital count: \(1\,(3s) + 3\,(3p) = 4\) orbitals in, 4 equivalent sp3 hybrid orbitals out. Each hybrid orbital holds one electron and forms one covalent bond, so silicon forms exactly 4 bonds.

docs.title: Problem 13
docs.text:
Explain, in your own words, the key structural difference between a polycrystalline solid and an amorphous solid.

Show Solution

A polycrystalline solid retains long-range periodic order, but only within each small grain, with grains meeting at grain boundaries and oriented differently from one another. An amorphous solid has no long-range periodic order at all, even within small regions, though its local atomic bonding is still roughly preserved.

docs.title: Problem 14
docs.text:
A silicon crystal has an extra silicon atom squeezed into the open space between four regular lattice sites, with all four regular sites still correctly occupied. Classify this defect.

Show Solution

This is an interstitial defect — an extra atom occupying a space between regular lattice sites, rather than sitting on a regular site itself.

docs.title: Problem 15
docs.text:
Explain why grain boundaries in polycrystalline silicon degrade electronic performance compared to single-crystal silicon.

Show Solution

Grain boundaries are thin, disordered regions where two differently-oriented periodic lattices meet; this disorder scatters charge carriers as they move through the material, reducing carrier mobility and overall electronic performance relative to a single, uninterrupted crystal.

docs.title: Problem 16
docs.text:
Explain qualitatively why two silicon atoms bond covalently with each other rather than ionically, even though both atoms are identical.

Show Solution

Ionic bonding requires a large electronegativity difference so that one atom donates and the other accepts electrons completely. Two identical silicon atoms have zero electronegativity difference between them, so there is no driving force for a complete electron transfer; instead, each atom contributes one electron to a shared pair, forming a covalent bond.

docs.title: Problem 17
docs.text:
Derive the tetrahedral bond angle from the geometric requirement that 4 identical directions from a common center be spaced as far apart as possible, showing that this angle is \(\arccos(-1/3)\).

Show Solution

Placing 4 identical unit vectors symmetrically so their sum is zero (each direction pulls equally, so the net electron-electron repulsion is balanced in every direction) is the geometric condition satisfied uniquely by the 4 vertex directions of a regular tetrahedron centered on the origin. Computing the dot product between any two such unit vectors gives \(\cos\theta = -1/3\), so \(\theta = \arccos(-1/3) \approx 109.47°\), matching the tetrahedral bond angle used throughout this chapter.

docs.title: Problem 18
docs.text:
A hypothetical ionic crystal has ions of charge \(+2e\) and \(-2e\) separated by \(r=0.24\) nm. Estimate its Coulomb bond energy in electron-volts, and compare it to the \(\text{Na}^+\text{Cl}^-\) result of about \(-5.1\) eV found in the chapter (charges of \(\pm e\) at \(r=0.28\) nm).

Show Solution

With charges \(\pm2e\): \(U(r) = -\dfrac{(8.99\times10^9)(2\times1.602\times10^{-19})^2}{0.24\times10^{-9}} = -3.85\times10^{-18}\ \text{J} \approx -24.0\ \text{eV}\). This is roughly 4.7 times more negative (stronger) than the \(\text{Na}^+\text{Cl}^-\) case, reflecting both the doubled charge on each ion (a factor of 4 in \(U\propto q_1q_2\)) and the slightly smaller separation.

docs.title: Problem 19
docs.text:
A larger fragment of a silicon crystal contains 20 interior silicon atoms, each fully bonded to 4 neighbors within the fragment (assume no bonds cross the fragment boundary). Find the total number of covalent bonds and the total number of shared electrons in the fragment.

Show Solution

Each of the 20 atoms contributes 4 bond-ends, giving \(20\times4=80\) bond-ends; since each bond has 2 ends, the number of distinct bonds is \(80/2=40\). Each bond shares 2 electrons, so the total shared electron count is \(40\times2=80\).

docs.title: Problem 20
docs.text:
Explain why amorphous silicon can still function reasonably well as a semiconductor for applications like thin-film solar cells, despite having no long-range periodic order — and identify which later chapter's core assumption this lack of order technically violates.

Show Solution

Amorphous silicon still preserves each atom's approximate 4-fold, tetrahedrally-coordinated local bonding environment, even though that local order does not repeat periodically over long distances. Since basic semiconducting behavior (light absorption, carrier generation) depends heavily on this short-range bonding, amorphous silicon remains usable, at some efficiency cost relative to single-crystal silicon. This lack of long-range periodicity technically violates the perfectly periodic potential that Chapter 5 assumes when solving the Schrödinger equation for an electron in a crystal — Chapter 5's energy-band theory strictly applies to single-crystal, defect-free material.

docs.title: Problem 21
docs.text:
A hypothetical element X has 2 valence electrons and low electronegativity. Predict whether element X, bonded with itself (X–X), is more likely to form a covalent, ionic, or metallic solid, and justify your answer using the reasoning framework developed in this chapter.

Show Solution

Low electronegativity means element X does not hold its valence electrons tightly, and with no electronegativity difference between identical X atoms there is no driving force for complete electron transfer (ruling out an ionic bond). With only 2 valence electrons — too few to conveniently form the multiple shared pairs a covalent network would require, and loosely held besides — X's valence electrons are more likely to delocalize into a shared electron sea, favoring a metallic bond, similar to the alkaline-earth metals (which also have 2 valence electrons and low electronegativity).

docs.title: Chapter 4 Quiz - Chemical Bonding in Semiconductor Crystals
Quiz: Chemical Bonding in Semiconductor Crystals
docs.text:
Test your understanding of the chemical bonding covered in Chapter 4 with these 20 questions.

Question 1

What is a valence electron?

  1. Any electron in an atom's nucleus
  2. An electron in an atom's outermost occupied shell, available for chemical bonding
  3. An electron that has been permanently removed from an atom
  4. A core electron tightly bound near the nucleus
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

A valence electron occupies an atom's outermost shell and is available to participate in chemical bonding. Silicon has 4 valence electrons, which determine its entire bonding behavior.

Concept Tested: Valence Electron

Question 2

How many valence electrons does a neutral silicon atom have?

  1. 1
  2. 2
  3. 4
  4. 14
Show Answer

Correct Answer: C

Silicon's electron configuration is \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^2\). The 10 electrons in the first two shells are core electrons; the 4 electrons in \(3s^2\,3p^2\) are valence electrons.

Concept Tested: Silicon Atom Structure

Question 3

What is silicon's full electron configuration?

  1. \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^2\)
  2. \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^1\)
  3. \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^5\)
  4. \(1s^2\,2s^2\)
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

Silicon (atomic number 14) has electron configuration \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^2\), giving it 10 core electrons and 4 valence electrons.

Concept Tested: Silicon Atom Structure

Question 4

What is a covalent bond?

  1. A bond formed by transferring an electron completely from one atom to another
  2. A bond formed when two atoms each contribute one valence electron to a shared electron pair
  3. A bond formed by delocalizing electrons across an entire crystal
  4. The force holding a nucleus together
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

A covalent bond forms when two atoms each contribute one valence electron to a shared pair, attracted electrostatically to both nuclei. It is the bond type used by silicon and germanium.

Concept Tested: Covalent Bond

Question 5

Why is a covalent bond described as directional?

  1. Because it points specifically along the line connecting the two specific atoms sharing the electron pair
  2. Because it pulls equally in every direction around each atom
  3. Because it has no fixed geometry at all
  4. Because it only exists in metals
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

A covalent bond's shared electron pair is localized between one specific pair of atoms, so the bond points along the line connecting those two nuclei — unlike ionic or metallic bonding, which are non-directional.

Concept Tested: Covalent Bond

Question 6

What is an ionic bond?

  1. A bond formed by sharing an electron pair between two atoms
  2. A bond formed when one atom transfers one or more valence electrons completely to another, producing oppositely charged ions
  3. A bond formed only between identical atoms
  4. A bond that only exists in gases
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

An ionic bond forms when one atom transfers electrons completely to another, producing a cation and an anion held together by Coulomb attraction — non-directional, unlike a covalent bond.

Concept Tested: Ionic Bond

Question 7

In the standard NaCl example, what happens to sodium's single valence electron?

  1. It is shared equally between the two atoms
  2. It delocalizes into an electron sea
  3. It is transferred completely to chlorine, producing \(\text{Na}^+\) and \(\text{Cl}^-\)
  4. It is destroyed
Show Answer

Correct Answer: C

Sodium's single valence electron transfers completely to chlorine, forming \(\text{Na}^+\) and \(\text{Cl}^-\), which then attract electrostatically to form the ionic bond.

Concept Tested: Ionic Bond

Question 8

Which equation gives the Coulomb potential energy of an ionic bond, at ion separation \(r\)?

  1. \(U(r) = -\dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\)
  2. \(U(r) = \dfrac{1}{2}kr^2\)
  3. \(U(r) = mc^2\)
  4. \(U(r) = qV\)
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

The ionic bond is simply the Coulomb potential energy between the two oppositely charged ions, \(U(r) = -e^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0 r)\), from Chapter 1's electrostatics.

Concept Tested: Ionic Bond

Question 9

What does the electron-sea model describe?

  1. Electrons transferred completely between two specific atoms
  2. Electrons shared between one specific pair of atoms
  3. Valence electrons delocalized across an entire crystal, surrounding fixed positive ion cores
  4. Electrons trapped permanently inside the nucleus
Show Answer

Correct Answer: C

In the electron-sea model of metallic bonding, valence electrons delocalize away from their parent atoms into a mobile sea surrounding fixed positive ion cores, belonging to the crystal as a whole.

Concept Tested: Metallic Bond

Question 10

Which two properties does the electron-sea model of metallic bonding directly explain?

  1. Brittleness and low melting point
  2. Electrical conductivity and malleability
  3. Directional bonding and high hardness
  4. Amorphous structure and grain boundaries
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Delocalized electrons are already free to move (explaining conductivity), and the non-directional electron sea redistributes as ion cores slide past one another under stress (explaining malleability).

Concept Tested: Metallic Bond

Question 11

Why does silicon bond covalently rather than metallically, despite both silicon and metals having valence electrons available for bonding?

  1. Silicon has 4 valence electrons, exactly enough to form 4 shared electron-pair bonds, rather than the loosely-bound 1-electron case that favors delocalization into an electron sea
  2. Silicon has no valence electrons at all
  3. Silicon's electrons cannot be shared under any circumstances
  4. Metals always have more protons than silicon
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

Silicon's 4 valence electrons are exactly the right number to form 4 shared electron-pair bonds, completing its octet — unlike copper's single, loosely-bound valence electron, which delocalizes readily into a metallic electron sea.

Concept Tested: Covalent Bond

Question 12

What is sp3 hybridization?

  1. The transfer of electrons between two atoms
  2. The combination of one \(s\) orbital and three \(p\) orbitals into four new, equivalent hybrid orbitals
  3. The delocalization of electrons into an electron sea
  4. A type of crystal defect
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

sp3 hybridization combines one \(s\) orbital and three \(p\) orbitals into four equivalent hybrid orbitals pointing toward the corners of a regular tetrahedron.

Concept Tested: Tetrahedral Bonding

Question 13

How many sp3 hybrid orbitals does silicon form from its valence orbitals?

  1. 1
  2. 2
  3. 3
  4. 4
Show Answer

Correct Answer: D

Silicon's one \(3s\) orbital and three \(3p\) orbitals combine into 4 equivalent sp3 hybrid orbitals, matching its 4 valence electrons and 4 covalent bonds.

Concept Tested: Tetrahedral Bonding

Question 14

What is the tetrahedral bond angle formed between silicon's sp3 hybrid orbitals?

  1. \(90°\)
  2. \(109.5°\)
  3. \(120°\)
  4. \(180°\)
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

The tetrahedral bond angle is \(\theta = \arccos(-1/3) \approx 109.5°\), the angle that maximizes separation between 4 identical directions from a common center.

Concept Tested: Tetrahedral Bonding

Question 15

How does tetrahedral bonding relate to the diamond lattice structure introduced in Chapter 3?

  1. It is unrelated to crystal geometry
  2. It is the chemical, first-principles explanation for the diamond lattice's coordination number of 4
  3. It explains why the diamond lattice has coordination number 12
  4. It only applies to metals
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Silicon's 4 tetrahedrally-arranged sp3 covalent bonds connect it to exactly 4 nearest neighbors, which is exactly the coordination number Chapter 3 verified geometrically for the diamond lattice structure.

Concept Tested: Tetrahedral Bonding

Question 16

What is an amorphous solid?

  1. A solid with perfect long-range periodic order throughout
  2. A solid with roughly preserved local bonding but no long-range periodic order
  3. A solid made of many single-crystal grains
  4. A solid with no atoms at all
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

An amorphous solid, such as amorphous silicon, preserves roughly the same local bonding environment a crystal would prefer, but has no long-range periodic order beyond a few atomic spacings.

Concept Tested: Amorphous Solid

Question 17

What is a polycrystalline solid?

  1. A single, perfectly periodic crystal with no boundaries
  2. A solid with no atoms arranged in any pattern
  3. A solid composed of many small single-crystal grains, each oriented differently, separated by grain boundaries
  4. A solid that only exists in liquids
Show Answer

Correct Answer: C

A polycrystalline solid, such as polysilicon, consists of many small grains, each internally a periodic single crystal, but randomly oriented relative to one another and separated by grain boundaries.

Concept Tested: Polycrystalline Solid

Question 18

Why is single-crystal silicon preferred over polycrystalline silicon for the active transistor regions of an integrated circuit?

  1. Polycrystalline silicon is more expensive
  2. Grain boundaries in polycrystalline silicon scatter charge carriers and degrade electronic performance
  3. Polycrystalline silicon has no valence electrons
  4. There is no difference in performance
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Grain boundaries are disordered regions that scatter charge carriers, degrading electronic performance — which is why active transistor regions use large single crystals, while polysilicon is reserved for gate electrodes and interconnects.

Concept Tested: Polycrystalline Solid

Question 19

Which of the following are the three basic types of point crystal defects?

  1. Covalent, ionic, and metallic
  2. Vacancy, interstitial, and substitutional
  3. Amorphous, polycrystalline, and single crystal
  4. Simple cubic, BCC, and FCC
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

The three basic point defects are a vacancy (a missing atom), an interstitial (an extra atom between regular sites), and a substitutional defect (a foreign atom replacing a host atom).

Concept Tested: Crystal Defect

Question 20

A phosphorus atom occupies a lattice site normally held by a silicon atom. What type of defect is this, and what later chapter deliberately exploits it?

  1. A vacancy defect, exploited in Chapter 5
  2. An interstitial defect, exploited in Chapter 6
  3. A substitutional defect, exploited by doping in Chapter 8
  4. Not a defect at all
Show Answer

Correct Answer: C

A foreign atom (phosphorus) occupying a regular lattice site normally held by the host atom (silicon) is a substitutional defect — exactly the mechanism deliberately exploited in Chapter 8's discussion of doping.

Concept Tested: Crystal Defect

docs.title: Chapter 5: Quantum Mechanics of Periodic Crystals
docs.text:
Chapter Overview (click to expand)

This chapter solves the Schrödinger equation, introduced in Chapter 2, for an electron moving through the periodic potential created by the crystal lattice and chemical bonding of Chapters 3 and 4. Bloch's theorem shows that the solutions must take a specific wavelike form, and the Kronig-Penney model — a simplified but exactly solvable periodic potential — shows explicitly how this periodicity forces electron energies to split into continuous allowed bands separated by forbidden band gaps. Along the way, the chapter introduces the reciprocal lattice and Brillouin zone, the standard mathematical tools used to describe a crystal's periodicity in momentum space, and shows that band gaps open precisely at Brillouin zone boundaries.

Key Takeaways:

  1. Chapter 4's chemical bonding produces the periodic lattice of Chapter 3; this periodicity means an electron in a crystal experiences a periodic potential energy \(V(x+a) = V(x)\), not the isolated, localized potentials of Chapter 2.
  2. Bloch's theorem states that the Schrödinger equation's solutions in any periodic potential must take the form \(\psi_k(x) = e^{ikx}u_k(x)\), where \(u_k(x)\) has the same periodicity as the lattice — a traveling wave modulated by a periodic function.
  3. The Kronig-Penney model — a periodic array of finite square barriers — is a simplified periodic potential that can be solved exactly, producing a transcendental equation relating energy \(E\) to a wavevector \(k\).
  4. Because the Kronig-Penney transcendental equation requires \(\cos(ka)\), a quantity restricted to \([-1,1]\), certain ranges of energy \(E\) have no valid solution at all — these forbidden ranges are band gaps, while the ranges that do have solutions are continuous energy bands of allowed energy states.
  5. The reciprocal lattice is a lattice in "k-space" (or momentum space) that describes a crystal's periodicity in the same natural units used by Bloch's theorem's wavevector \(k\); it is mathematically derived from, but geometrically distinct from, the real-space lattice of Chapter 3.
  6. The Brillouin zone is the primitive cell of the reciprocal lattice; the Kronig-Penney model's band gaps open precisely at the Brillouin zone boundaries, \(k=\pm n\pi/a\), giving reciprocal-space meaning to where bands split.
  7. Solving the periodic-potential problem is called band formation; the resulting bands are conventionally labeled by function — the highest band fully occupied by electrons at absolute zero is the valence band, and the next-higher, largely empty band is the conduction band.
  8. This chapter's band-formation physics is the foundation for Chapter 6's direct treatment of band structure, effective mass, and density of states, and ultimately for Chapter 7's classification of materials as insulators, semiconductors, or conductors based on the size of the band gap between these two bands.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Explain why an electron in a crystal experiences a periodic potential, and why this periodicity requires new mathematics beyond Chapter 2's isolated potential wells
  • State Bloch's theorem and interpret the meaning of the Bloch wavevector \(k\) and the periodic function \(u_k(x)\)
  • Describe the Kronig-Penney model's periodic potential and set up its solution using the boundary conditions at each barrier
  • Explain, using the Kronig-Penney transcendental equation, why certain energy ranges are allowed and others forbidden
  • Define the reciprocal lattice and compute reciprocal lattice vectors from a set of real-space lattice vectors
  • Define the Brillouin zone as the primitive cell of the reciprocal lattice, and identify the first Brillouin zone boundary for a 1D lattice
  • Connect the location of band gaps directly to the Brillouin zone boundaries
  • Distinguish an energy band, a band gap, and the allowed and forbidden energy states within them
  • Distinguish the valence band from the conduction band and state which is higher in energy
  • Solve worked and practice problems combining these ideas, in preparation for the effective-mass and density-of-states discussions of Chapter 6

How to read this chapter

This chapter is mathematically the most demanding one so far, but its central physical idea is simple: periodicity forces energy into bands. Chapters 3 and 4 explained where atoms sit and why they bond the way they do; this chapter finally asks what that arrangement does to an electron's allowed energies. The Kronig-Penney model is worked through in enough detail to see exactly how the band structure emerges mathematically, but you are not expected to reproduce every algebraic step from memory — focus instead on the qualitative shape of the result (bands separated by gaps, gaps at zone boundaries) since that shape, not the specific transcendental equation, is what every later chapter relies on.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Chapter 2 solved the Schrödinger equation for isolated, idealized potentials — a single infinite well, a single finite well, a single barrier. Chapter 3 then described the precise geometric arrangement of atoms in a real crystal, and Chapter 4 explained the chemical bonding forces that hold those atoms in that arrangement. Putting these threads together, an electron moving through an actual crystal does not see an isolated potential at all: it sees the electrostatic potential energy of every atomic core in the lattice, repeating with exactly the periodicity Chapter 3 established. This chapter solves the Schrödinger equation for exactly this situation — a periodic potential, \(V(x+a)=V(x)\), where \(a\) is the lattice constant — and shows that the result is qualitatively different from anything in Chapter 2.

The key mathematical tool is Bloch's theorem, which shows that any solution to the Schrödinger equation in a periodic potential must take a specific form: a traveling wave, \(e^{ikx}\), multiplied by a function \(u_k(x)\) that repeats with the same periodicity as the lattice itself. This theorem does not, by itself, solve for the allowed energies — it only constrains the form the solution must take. To actually compute allowed energies, this chapter uses the Kronig-Penney model, a periodic potential simple enough (a repeating series of finite rectangular barriers) to solve exactly. The Kronig-Penney model's solution takes the form of a transcendental equation, and the key discovery is that this equation can only be satisfied for certain ranges of energy \(E\) — other ranges are mathematically forbidden entirely. The allowed ranges are called energy bands, and the forbidden ranges between them are called band gaps. This splitting of continuous free-particle energy into bands and gaps, called band formation, is the single most important result of this chapter, and the physical basis for every subsequent chapter's treatment of semiconductors.

Describing exactly where these bands and gaps occur requires one more set of tools: the reciprocal lattice and the Brillouin zone. Bloch's theorem describes solutions using the wavevector \(k\), which has units of inverse length — the same units used to describe a crystal's periodicity in "k-space," or momentum space. The reciprocal lattice is precisely this k-space description of a crystal's periodicity, constructed mathematically from the real-space lattice vectors of Chapter 3 but generally different in geometry from the real lattice itself. The Brillouin zone is the primitive cell of this reciprocal lattice — the k-space analog of Chapter 3's primitive cell — and this chapter's central geometric result is that the Kronig-Penney model's band gaps open exactly at the Brillouin zone boundaries.

Finally, the chapter introduces the terminology used to describe the resulting bands: at absolute zero temperature, electrons fill the lowest available energy bands first, so the highest band that ends up completely full is called the valence band, and the next band up — typically empty at absolute zero — is called the conduction band. Whether a material behaves as an insulator, a semiconductor, or a conductor turns out to depend almost entirely on the size of the band gap separating these two bands, and on whether any band is only partially filled — the subject of Chapter 7.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This chapter builds on Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations, particularly the Schrödinger equation, wavefunctions, and eigenvalues, and on Chapter 3: Crystal Lattices and Structures, particularly the lattice constant and the periodic geometric arrangement of atoms that gives rise to the periodic potential this chapter solves.

docs.title: The Periodic Potential and Bloch's Theorem
Why a Crystal's Potential Is Periodic
docs.text:
Chapter 2's Schrödinger equation, \(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2\psi}{dx^2}+V(x)\psi=E\psi\), was solved there for potentials \(V(x)\) describing a single isolated feature: one infinite wall, one finite well, one barrier. A real crystal is nothing like this. Chapter 3 showed that a crystal is an essentially infinite, perfectly periodic arrangement of atoms, spaced by the lattice constant \(a\); Chapter 4 showed that each of those atoms holds onto its electrons, and bonds to its neighbors, through electrostatic forces identical in kind to the ones that create any atomic potential well. An electron moving through this crystal therefore experiences the combined electrostatic potential of every atomic core in the lattice, and because the lattice itself is periodic, so is this potential energy function:

\[ V(x+a) = V(x) \]

This single equation is the starting point for the entire chapter: whatever solves the Schrödinger equation in a crystal must do so subject to this periodicity constraint, a fundamentally different requirement from any potential solved in Chapter 2.

docs.title: Bloch's Theorem
docs.text:
Bloch's theorem states that any solution to the Schrödinger equation for a periodic potential satisfying \(V(x+a)=V(x)\) must take the form:

\[ \psi_k(x) = e^{ikx}\,u_k(x), \qquad u_k(x+a) = u_k(x) \]

That is, the wavefunction is a plane wave \(e^{ikx}\) (a traveling wave, similar in form to the free-particle wavefunctions encountered in Chapter 2's discussion of wave packets) multiplied by a function \(u_k(x)\) that repeats with exactly the same periodicity as the lattice itself. The quantity \(k\) is called the Bloch wavevector, and \(\hbar k\) is often called the electron's crystal momentum — it behaves like momentum in many respects (it appears in group-velocity and semiclassical equations of motion used in later chapters) but, unlike true momentum, it is only meaningful modulo a reciprocal lattice vector, a subtlety this chapter returns to once the reciprocal lattice has been defined.

Bloch's theorem is powerful but incomplete on its own: it constrains the form of every solution, but it does not by itself say which energies \(E\) are actually achievable. To answer that question — the central question of this chapter — requires an explicit, solvable periodic potential, which is exactly what the Kronig-Penney model provides.

flowchart LR
    A["Periodic Potential<br/>V(x+a) = V(x)"] --> B["Bloch's Theorem"]
    B --> C["psi_k(x) = e^(ikx) u_k(x)<br/>u_k periodic"]
    C --> D["Solve for allowed E(k):<br/>Kronig-Penney Model"]

docs.title: Setting Up a Solvable Periodic Potential
docs.text:
The Kronig-Penney model replaces the true, complicated periodic potential of a real crystal with the simplest periodic potential that can still be solved exactly: an infinite, repeating series of rectangular potential barriers, each of height \(V_0\) and width \(b\), separated by wells of width \(a-b\) where the electron moves freely. This is a direct periodic-potential analog of the finite potential well Chapter 2 already solved, repeated infinitely with period \(a\).

Inside each well, the electron's wavefunction is an oscillating solution (as in the free regions of Chapter 2's finite well), and inside each barrier, the wavefunction is an exponentially decaying/growing solution (as in Chapter 2's quantum tunneling discussion) — the difference here is that Bloch's theorem must additionally be imposed at the boundary between neighboring periods, linking the solution in one cell to the solution in the next via the factor \(e^{ika}\).

docs.title: The Kronig-Penney Transcendental Equation
docs.text:
Applying the wavefunction and derivative continuity conditions at each boundary, together with Bloch's theorem's periodicity requirement, produces the model's central result — a single transcendental equation relating the electron's energy (through a wavenumber \(\alpha=\sqrt{2mE}/\hbar\) inside the wells) to the Bloch wavevector \(k\):

\[ P\,\frac{\sin(\alpha a)}{\alpha a} + \cos(\alpha a) = \cos(ka) \]

where \(P\) is a dimensionless constant proportional to the barrier strength (increasing with barrier height \(V_0\) and width \(b\)), often written \(P = m V_0 b a/\hbar^2\) in the idealized limit of thin, tall barriers (\(b\to0\), \(V_0\to\infty\), with \(V_0 b\) held fixed). This equation is the mathematical heart of the entire chapter, and its structure is what produces band formation, explained next.

docs.title: Why Certain Energies Are Forbidden
docs.text:
The right-hand side of the transcendental equation, \(\cos(ka)\), is a cosine of a real number, and therefore can only ever take values between \(-1\) and \(+1\). The left-hand side, however, is a specific function of energy \(E\) (through \(\alpha\)) that is not restricted to this range — for many values of \(\alpha a\), the left-hand side evaluates to something greater than \(+1\) or less than \(-1\). Whenever this happens, there is no real value of \(k\) that can satisfy the equation, because no real \(k\) produces a cosine outside \([-1,1]\). That range of energy is therefore physically forbidden to the electron — a band gap, or forbidden energy gap. Wherever the left-hand side does fall within \([-1,1]\), a real \(k\) exists, and — because \(k\) can vary continuously within this range — that range of energy forms a continuous energy band of allowed energy states. This alternating pattern of bands and gaps, repeating as energy increases, is what this chapter calls band formation.

Concept Check

In the limit \(P \to 0\) (very weak or vanishing barriers), the Kronig-Penney transcendental equation reduces to \(\cos(\alpha a) = \cos(ka)\), which has a solution \(k=\alpha\) for every value of \(\alpha\). What does this limit physically represent, and are there any band gaps in it?

Concept Check — click to reveal answer

As \(P\to0\), the barriers vanish and the periodic potential becomes flat — the electron is simply a free particle. In this limit, every energy \(E=\hbar^2\alpha^2/2m\) is achievable for some real \(k\), so there are no forbidden gaps at all: the allowed energies form one continuous band, exactly like a free particle's continuous energy spectrum. Band gaps only appear once \(P>0\), confirming that the periodic potential itself — not some separate effect — is the direct cause of band formation.

docs.title: Definition and Construction
docs.text:
To describe where in \(k\)-space the Kronig-Penney model's bands and gaps occur, it is useful to define a lattice not in real space but in the space of wavevectors \(k\) — this is the reciprocal lattice. Given a set of real-space primitive lattice vectors \(\vec a_1, \vec a_2, \vec a_3\) (Chapter 3), the reciprocal lattice vectors \(\vec b_1, \vec b_2, \vec b_3\) are defined by the orthogonality condition:

\[ \vec a_i \cdot \vec b_j = 2\pi\,\delta_{ij} \]

where \(\delta_{ij}\) is 1 if \(i=j\) and 0 otherwise. In one dimension, this reduces to a single, simple relationship: for a 1D chain with real-space lattice constant \(a\), the reciprocal lattice is itself a 1D lattice of points spaced by \(2\pi/a\). This spacing, \(2\pi/a\), is exactly the periodicity that appears throughout the Kronig-Penney analysis (for instance, in the location of the band gaps, discussed below).

The reciprocal lattice of a three-dimensional crystal is generally not geometrically identical to its real-space lattice. A well-known result, useful for connecting back to Chapter 3, is that the reciprocal lattice of an FCC (face-centered cubic) real-space lattice is a BCC (body-centered cubic) lattice, and vice versa — while the reciprocal lattice of a simple cubic lattice with constant \(a\) is itself simple cubic, with constant \(2\pi/a\).

Real-space lattice (Ch. 3) Reciprocal lattice Simple Cubic, constant \(a\) Simple Cubic, constant \(2\pi/a\) Face-Centered Cubic (FCC) Body-Centered Cubic (BCC) Body-Centered Cubic (BCC) Face-Centered Cubic (FCC)

docs.title: Reciprocal Lattice Vectors and Diffraction Notation
docs.text:
Reciprocal lattice vectors are also exactly the vectors used to index the Miller-index planes of Chapter 3: a reciprocal lattice vector \(\vec G_{hkl} = h\vec b_1 + k\vec b_2 + l\vec b_3\) points perpendicular to the real-space \((hkl)\) crystal plane, with magnitude inversely proportional to the spacing between adjacent \((hkl)\) planes — a direct, practically important link between the real-space crystallography of Chapter 3 and the momentum-space description this chapter introduces.

Worked Example 1 — Reciprocal Lattice Spacing

A 1D chain of atoms has lattice constant \(a = 0.30\) nm. Find the spacing of its reciprocal lattice.

Solution: The reciprocal lattice spacing is \(2\pi/a = 2\pi/(0.30\times10^{-9}\ \text{m}) \approx 2.09\times10^{10}\ \text{m}^{-1}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Brillouin zone is defined as the primitive cell of the reciprocal lattice — the k-space analog of Chapter 3's primitive cell, constructed by the same Wigner-Seitz procedure (the region of k-space closer to a given reciprocal lattice point than to any other). The first Brillouin zone is this primitive cell centered on \(k=0\); for a 1D chain of lattice constant \(a\), the first Brillouin zone is simply the interval:

\[ -\frac{\pi}{a} \leq k \leq \frac{\pi}{a} \]

Because the reciprocal lattice has spacing \(2\pi/a\), the first Brillouin zone boundary sits at exactly half that spacing, \(\pi/a\), on either side of the origin — directly analogous to how a 1D real-space Wigner-Seitz cell extends half a lattice constant on either side of a lattice point.

docs.title: Band Gaps Open at the Brillouin Zone Boundary
docs.text:
The chapter's central geometric result connects the Kronig-Penney model directly to the Brillouin zone: solving the Kronig-Penney transcendental equation in detail shows that the forbidden energy gaps occur precisely at the values \(k = \pm n\pi/a\) for integer \(n\) — exactly the Brillouin zone boundaries (the first Brillouin zone boundary at \(n=1\), the second at \(n=2\), and so on). This is not a coincidence: at these special \(k\) values, the electron's wave reflects constructively off the periodic lattice (an effect closely related to the Bragg-type reflection condition for waves in a periodic medium), and this standing-wave condition is exactly what opens an energy gap. Physically, this means the reciprocal lattice and Brillouin zone are not just bookkeeping devices — they directly predict where in k-space a real crystal's band gaps will appear.

    A["Reciprocal Lattice<br/>spacing 2*pi/a"] --> B["Brillouin Zone<br/>primitive cell of<br/>reciprocal lattice"]
    B --> C["1st BZ boundary:<br/>k = +/- pi/a"]
    C --> D["Kronig-Penney band gaps<br/>open exactly at these k values"]

Worked Example 2 — First Brillouin Zone Boundary

Find the first Brillouin zone boundary, in units of m\(^{-1}\), for silicon's diamond-cubic conventional lattice constant \(a=0.543\) nm, treated as a 1D chain of the same spacing for this estimate.

Solution: \(k_{\text{boundary}} = \pi/a = \pi/(0.543\times10^{-9}\ \text{m}) \approx 5.79\times10^{9}\ \text{m}^{-1}\).

docs.title: Energy Bands, Band Gaps, and Band Formation
Naming the Bands
docs.text:
Once the Kronig-Penney model (or any more realistic periodic-potential calculation) has been solved, the result is a set of continuous energy bands, each spanning a range of allowed energies, separated by forbidden band gaps. At absolute zero temperature, electrons fill these bands from the lowest energy upward, obeying the Pauli exclusion principle (introduced formally through Fermi-Dirac statistics in Chapter 9), until all available electrons are placed. This filling process gives the bands their physically important names:

Term Meaning Energy Band A continuous range of allowed electron energies, arising from band formation in a periodic potential Band Gap (Forbidden Energy Gap) A range of energy with no allowed electron states, lying between two energy bands Allowed Energy States The specific, continuously-varying \((E,k)\) pairs that satisfy the periodic Schrödinger equation within a band Valence Band The highest energy band that is completely filled with electrons at absolute zero Conduction Band The next energy band above the valence band, typically empty (or nearly so) at absolute zero

The valence and conduction bands are singled out for special attention because, as Chapter 7 will show in detail, essentially all of a semiconductor's electrical behavior — its conductivity, its response to doping, its behavior in a diode or transistor — is governed by electrons and holes in exactly these two bands and the size of the band gap separating them.

Concept Check

Explain why the valence band is, by definition, always the band immediately below the band gap that separates it from the conduction band, rather than some lower-lying, already fully-occupied band.

Concept Check — click to reveal answer

"Valence band" is not simply any filled band — it is specifically the highest-energy filled band at absolute zero, because it is the electrons in this band (closest in energy to the gap and to the conduction band above) that participate in bonding and, more importantly, that can be thermally or optically excited across the gap into the conduction band. Lower-lying, more tightly bound bands (corresponding to core electrons, in the language of Chapter 4) are completely inert for this purpose, so the valence-band label is reserved for the outermost filled band specifically because that is the band whose electrons determine the material's electrical and chemical behavior.

Worked Example 3 — Identifying Bands from a Filling Description

A hypothetical 1D crystal's Kronig-Penney solution produces three energy bands, labeled I (lowest), II (middle), and III (highest). At absolute zero, bands I and II are completely full of electrons, and band III is completely empty. Identify the valence band and the conduction band.

Solution: The valence band is the highest completely filled band, which is band II. The conduction band is the next band up, band III.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter solved the Schrödinger equation for the periodic potential created by a real crystal lattice (Chapter 3) and its chemical bonding (Chapter 4). Bloch's theorem showed that every solution must take the form \(\psi_k(x)=e^{ikx}u_k(x)\), a traveling wave modulated by a lattice-periodic function, introducing the Bloch wavevector \(k\) and crystal momentum \(\hbar k\). The Kronig-Penney model, an exactly solvable periodic array of rectangular barriers, produced a transcendental equation, \(P\sin(\alpha a)/(\alpha a)+\cos(\alpha a)=\cos(ka)\), whose right-hand side's restriction to \([-1,1]\) directly explained band formation: energies where the equation has no real solution become forbidden band gaps, and energies where it does become continuous allowed energy bands. The reciprocal lattice and Brillouin zone provided the natural k-space language for this result, and the chapter's key geometric finding was that band gaps open precisely at the Brillouin zone boundaries \(k=\pm n\pi/a\). Finally, the highest completely-filled band at absolute zero was named the valence band, and the next band up the conduction band — terminology that Chapters 6 and 7 build on directly. With band formation now established, Chapter 6 turns to the detailed shape of these bands (direct vs. indirect gaps, effective mass, density of states) and locates the Fermi level within them.

docs.title: Key Equations
docs.text: Concept Equation Periodic potential \(V(x+a) = V(x)\) Bloch's theorem \(\psi_k(x) = e^{ikx}\,u_k(x)\), with \(u_k(x+a)=u_k(x)\) Kronig-Penney transcendental equation \(P\,\dfrac{\sin(\alpha a)}{\alpha a} + \cos(\alpha a) = \cos(ka)\) Reciprocal lattice vector condition \(\vec a_i\cdot\vec b_j = 2\pi\,\delta_{ij}\) 1D reciprocal lattice spacing \(2\pi/a\) First Brillouin zone (1D) \(-\pi/a \leq k \leq \pi/a\) Band gap locations (1D) \(k = \pm n\pi/a,\ n=1,2,3,\ldots\)
