docs.title: Worked Examples
docs.text:
Worked Example 7 — Heavy vs. Light Effective Mass

Two conduction bands have curvatures \(d^2E/dk^2\) differing by a factor of 4, with band A's curvature four times larger than band B's. Which band has the larger effective mass, and by what factor?

Solution: Since \(m^*=\hbar^2/(d^2E/dk^2)\), effective mass is inversely proportional to curvature. Band B, with the smaller curvature, has the larger effective mass — specifically four times larger than band A's, since \(m_B^*/m_A^*=(d^2E/dk^2)_A/(d^2E/dk^2)_B=4\).

Worked Example 8 — Photon Energy for a Direct-Gap Transition

GaAs has a direct band gap of \(1.42\) eV. Find the maximum wavelength of light that can be absorbed by a direct, band-edge transition.

Solution: The photon energy must be at least \(E_g\), so the maximum (threshold) wavelength satisfies \(E_g = hc/\lambda\):

\[ \lambda = \frac{hc}{E_g} = \frac{(4.136\times10^{-15}\ \text{eV}\cdot\text{s})(3.0\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s})}{1.42\ \text{eV}} \approx 8.7\times10^{-7}\ \text{m} = 870\ \text{nm} \]

This near-infrared threshold wavelength is why GaAs-based LEDs and laser diodes commonly emit in this range.

Worked Example 9 — Density of States Ratio

Compare the density of states at the same energy \(E-E_c\) above the band edge for two materials with electron effective masses \(m_1^*=0.067\,m_0\) (GaAs) and \(m_2^*=0.26\,m_0\) (Si).

Solution: Since \(g_c(E)\propto (m^*)^{3/2}\) at fixed \(E-E_c\):

\[ \frac{g_{c,\text{Si}}}{g_{c,\text{GaAs}}} = \left(\frac{0.26}{0.067}\right)^{3/2} \approx (3.88)^{1.5} \approx 7.6 \]

Silicon's heavier conduction-band effective mass gives it roughly 7.6 times more available conduction-band states at the same energy above the band edge than GaAs.

Worked Example 10 — Fermi Level Inside a Band (Metal) vs. Inside a Gap (Semiconductor)

For each case below, state whether the material is better described as a metal or a semiconductor/insulator: (a) \(E_F\) lies 2 eV above the bottom of a partially-filled band; (b) \(E_F\) lies exactly at the midpoint of a 1.1 eV gap between a full valence band and empty conduction band.

Solution: (a) A Fermi level inside a band, with real occupied and empty states immediately adjacent in energy, is the defining condition for a metal. (b) A Fermi level inside a gap, with a full valence band below and empty conduction band above, is the defining condition for the semiconductor/insulator category — and with a gap this small (1.1 eV, close to silicon's), specifically a semiconductor.

Worked Example 11 — Distinguishing Semimetal from Semiconductor

Material X has zero band gap — its valence and conduction bands touch at a single point in k-space, with essentially no density of states exactly at that energy, and it conducts weakly at all temperatures, including near absolute zero. Is Material X better classified as a metal, an insulator, or a semimetal?

Solution: A metal would have a substantial density of states at \(E_F\) (a genuinely partially-filled band); an insulator would have a large gap and negligible conduction at low temperature. Material X's near-zero gap combined with very low density of states at the band-touching point, and its weak-but-nonzero conduction even near absolute zero, is precisely the semimetal signature.

docs.title: Chapter 6 Glossary
docs.text: Terms introduced in Chapter 6 — Band Structure and the Fermi Level. See the full site Glossary for terms across all chapters.

docs.title: Density of States
docs.text:
The function \(g(E)\), defined so that \(g(E)\,dE\) is the number of allowed electron states per unit volume with energy between \(E\) and \(E+dE\).

Example: For a parabolic conduction band, \(g_c(E) = \frac{1}{2\pi^2}\left(\frac{2m_e^*}{\hbar^2}\right)^{3/2}\sqrt{E-E_c}\), growing as the square root of energy above the band edge.

See also: Effective Mass, Energy Band.

docs.title: Direct Bandgap
docs.text:
A band structure in which the conduction-band minimum and valence-band maximum occur at the same crystal momentum \(k\).

Example: GaAs is a direct-gap material, so a photon alone can drive a vertical, momentum-conserving transition between its band edges — the physical basis for efficient LEDs and laser diodes.

See also: Indirect Bandgap, E-K Diagram.

docs.title: E-K Diagram
docs.text:
A plot of allowed electron energy \(E\) versus crystal momentum (Bloch wavevector) \(k\), showing the detailed shape of a material's energy bands.

Example: An E-k diagram immediately reveals whether a material is direct- or indirect-gap by comparing the k-location of the conduction-band minimum to that of the valence-band maximum.

See also: Direct Bandgap, Indirect Bandgap, Bloch Theorem.

docs.title: Effective Mass
docs.text:
A quantity \(m^* = \hbar^2/(d^2E/dk^2)\), defined from the curvature of a band at an extremum, that lets an electron or hole there be treated with ordinary Newtonian mechanics.

Example: GaAs's sharply-curved conduction band gives it a small electron effective mass (\(m_e^*\approx0.067\,m_0\)), while silicon's more gently-curved conduction band gives it a larger one (\(m_e^*\approx0.26\,m_0\)).

See also: E-K Diagram, Density of States.

docs.title: Fermi Energy
docs.text:
The zero-temperature value of the Fermi level, equal to the energy of the highest occupied electron state.

Example: In a metal at \(T=0\), every state below the Fermi energy is completely filled and every state above it is completely empty.

See also: Fermi Level.

docs.title: Fermi Level
docs.text:
The parameter \(E_F\) in the Fermi-Dirac distribution \(f(E)=1/[1+\exp((E-E_F)/k_BT)]\) at any temperature, equal to the energy at which the occupation probability is exactly \(1/2\).

Example: In an intrinsic semiconductor, the Fermi level sits inside the band gap — where the density of states is zero — even though no electron actually has that exact energy.

See also: Fermi Energy, Density of States.

docs.title: Indirect Bandgap
docs.text:
A band structure in which the conduction-band minimum and valence-band maximum occur at different crystal momenta \(k\).

Example: Silicon is an indirect-gap material; a band-edge transition requires a phonon to supply the crystal-momentum difference \(\Delta k\) in addition to a photon, making silicon a much weaker light emitter than a direct-gap material.

See also: Direct Bandgap, E-K Diagram.

docs.title: Insulator Band Structure
docs.text:
A band structure with a completely full valence band and completely empty conduction band at absolute zero, separated by a large band gap (roughly greater than 4 eV) that prevents significant thermal excitation of carriers.

Example: Diamond, with a band gap of about 5.5 eV, is classified as an insulator under this definition.

See also: Semiconductor Band Structure, Metal Band Structure.

docs.title: Metal Band Structure
docs.text:
A band structure in which the Fermi level lies inside a partially-filled band, or in which the valence and conduction bands overlap in energy so that electrons partially occupy both.

Example: Magnesium conducts well despite having two valence electrons per atom (which naive electron counting would fill exactly one band) because its bands overlap in energy, leaving the Fermi level inside a partially-filled band.

See also: Insulator Band Structure, Semimetal.

docs.title: Semiconductor Band Structure
docs.text:
A band structure identical in kind to an insulator's — a completely full valence band and completely empty conduction band at absolute zero — but with a small enough band gap (roughly 0.1 to 3 eV) that a technologically significant number of carriers are thermally excited across it at room temperature.

Example: Silicon (\(E_g\approx1.12\) eV) and GaAs (\(E_g\approx1.42\) eV) are both classified as semiconductors under this definition.

See also: Insulator Band Structure, Fermi Level.

docs.title: Semimetal
docs.text:
A band structure in which the valence and conduction bands touch or slightly overlap in energy, but with very little density of states at the point of overlap, giving a much lower carrier density than a true metal.

Example: Bismuth and graphite are classified as semimetals: they conduct at all temperatures, unlike an insulator, but far more weakly than a true metal.

See also: Metal Band Structure, Density of States.

docs.title: Chapter 6 Problems - Band Structure and the Fermi Level
End-of-Chapter Problems: Band Structure and the Fermi Level
docs.text: Work through these problems to reinforce your understanding of band structure, effective mass, density of states, and the Fermi level covered in Chapter 6.

docs.title: Problem 1
docs.text:
Define, in one sentence each, a direct bandgap and an indirect bandgap.

Show Solution

A direct bandgap material has its conduction-band minimum and valence-band maximum at the same crystal momentum \(k\). An indirect bandgap material has them at different crystal momenta.

docs.title: Problem 2
docs.text:
State the formula defining effective mass in terms of band curvature.

Show Solution

\(\dfrac{1}{m^*} = \dfrac{1}{\hbar^2}\dfrac{d^2E}{dk^2}\).

docs.title: Problem 3
docs.text:
What physical question does the density of states \(g(E)\) answer?

Show Solution

How many allowed electron states exist per unit volume in a small energy range near \(E\) — \(g(E)\,dE\) is the number of states per unit volume between \(E\) and \(E+dE\).

docs.title: Problem 4
docs.text:
State the Fermi-Dirac distribution.

Show Solution

\(f(E) = \dfrac{1}{1+\exp\left(\frac{E-E_F}{k_BT}\right)}\).

docs.title: Problem 5
docs.text:
Distinguish the Fermi level from the Fermi energy in one or two sentences.

Show Solution

The Fermi level \(E_F\) is the general parameter in the Fermi-Dirac distribution at any temperature, and can lie inside a band gap where no states exist. The Fermi energy is specifically its \(T=0\) value, equal to the energy of the highest occupied state.

docs.title: Problem 6
docs.text:
List the four material categories produced by band-structure classification.

Show Solution

Metal, insulator, semiconductor, and semimetal.

docs.title: Problem 7
docs.text:
Is silicon a direct or indirect bandgap material? What about GaAs?

Show Solution

Silicon is indirect (conduction-band minimum away from \(k=0\), valence-band maximum at \(k=0\)). GaAs is direct (both extrema at \(k=0\)).

docs.title: Problem 8
docs.text:
What condition on the Fermi level defines a metal band structure?

Show Solution

The Fermi level lies inside a band that is only partially filled (or inside a region where two bands overlap in energy), so there are empty states immediately adjacent in energy to filled ones.

docs.title: Problem 9
docs.text:
A valence band near its maximum is described by \(E(k) = E_v - \beta k^2\), with \(\beta = 1.2\times10^{-37}\ \text{J}\cdot\text{m}^2\). Find the hole effective mass \(m_h^*\) in units of \(m_0=9.11\times10^{-31}\) kg.

Show Solution

Comparing to \(E(k)=E_v-\hbar^2k^2/(2m_h^*)\) gives \(\beta=\hbar^2/(2m_h^*)\), so \(m_h^*=\hbar^2/(2\beta) = (1.055\times10^{-34})^2/(2\times1.2\times10^{-37}) \approx 4.63\times10^{-32}\ \text{kg} \approx 0.051\,m_0\).

docs.title: Problem 10
docs.text:
Two conduction bands have effective masses \(m_A^*=0.10\,m_0\) and \(m_B^*=0.40\,m_0\). Find the ratio \(g_{c,B}(E)/g_{c,A}(E)\) at the same energy above their respective band edges.

Show Solution

Since \(g_c(E)\propto(m^*)^{3/2}\): \(g_{c,B}/g_{c,A} = (0.40/0.10)^{3/2} = 4^{1.5} = 8\). Band B has 8 times more available states at the same energy above its edge.

docs.title: Problem 11
docs.text:
Explain why an indirect band-to-band transition requires a phonon in addition to a photon.

Show Solution

A photon carries negligible crystal momentum compared to typical electron crystal momenta, so it can only drive a nearly vertical (\(\Delta k\approx0\)) transition. In an indirect-gap material, the conduction-band minimum and valence-band maximum are offset in \(k\), so completing the transition requires a phonon to supply or absorb the missing crystal momentum \(\Delta k\).

docs.title: Problem 12
docs.text:
A crystal has a completely full valence band and completely empty conduction band at \(T=0\), separated by a gap of \(0.67\) eV. Classify this material.

Show Solution

A full valence band and empty conduction band place it in the insulator/semiconductor category; a gap this small (\(0.67\) eV, close to germanium's actual gap) is small enough for significant room-temperature thermal excitation, so this material is a semiconductor.

docs.title: Problem 13
docs.text:
A conduction-band state sits \(0.10\) eV above the Fermi level at \(T=300\) K (\(k_BT\approx0.0259\) eV). Estimate its occupation probability.

Show Solution

Since \(E-E_F\gg k_BT\): \(f(E)\approx\exp(-0.10/0.0259)=\exp(-3.86)\approx0.021\). About 2 states in 100 at this energy are occupied.

docs.title: Problem 14
docs.text:
A hypothetical direct-gap material has \(E_g=2.0\) eV. Find the maximum wavelength of light that can be absorbed by a direct band-edge transition.

Show Solution

\(\lambda = hc/E_g = (4.136\times10^{-15}\ \text{eV}\cdot\text{s})(3.0\times10^8\ \text{m/s})/2.0\ \text{eV} \approx 6.2\times10^{-7}\ \text{m} = 620\ \text{nm} (visible red light).

docs.title: Problem 15
docs.text:
Explain, physically, why a semimetal conducts electricity at all temperatures (including near absolute zero) while an insulator does not.

Show Solution

In a semimetal, the valence and conduction bands touch or slightly overlap in energy, so a small number of states above the nominal band edge are genuinely, permanently occupied (and a small number below are genuinely, permanently empty) even at \(T=0\) — no thermal excitation across a gap is required. An insulator has a real gap with zero density of states in between, so at \(T=0\) the valence band is exactly full and the conduction band is exactly empty, with no carriers available at all.

docs.title: Problem 16
docs.text:
Band X has curvature \(d^2E/dk^2\) four times larger than Band Y's. Which band has electrons that respond more sluggishly to an applied electric field, and why?

Show Solution

Band Y, with the smaller curvature, has the larger effective mass (\(m^*=\hbar^2/(d^2E/dk^2)\) is inversely proportional to curvature), and a larger effective mass means the electron accelerates more slowly under the same applied force, \(F=m^*a\) — so Band Y's electrons respond more sluggishly.

docs.title: Problem 17
docs.text:
Starting from the k-space counting argument \(g(k)\,dk = k^2\,dk/\pi^2\) (states per unit volume, including spin) and the parabolic relation \(E-E_c=\hbar^2k^2/2m_e^*\), derive the conduction-band density of states \(g_c(E)\), showing each substitution step.

Show Solution

From \(E-E_c=\hbar^2k^2/2m_e^*\), solve for \(k=\sqrt{2m_e^*(E-E_c)}/\hbar\) and differentiate to get \(dk/dE = \sqrt{2m_e^*}/(2\hbar\sqrt{E-E_c})\). Requiring \(g(k)\,dk=g_c(E)\,dE\) gives \(g_c(E)=\frac{k^2}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac{dk}{dE}\). Substituting both expressions and simplifying the algebra yields \(g_c(E)=\frac{1}{2\pi^2}\left(\frac{2m_e^*}{\hbar^2}\right)^{3/2}\sqrt{E-E_c}\), matching the chapter's result.

docs.title: Problem 18
docs.text:
A metal's electrons can be modeled, at \(T=0\), as filling a free-electron-like conduction band up to the Fermi energy, with electron density \(n\) related to \(E_F\) by \(n=\int_0^{E_F}g_c(E)\,dE\) using \(m_e^*=m_0\). Show that this integral gives \(E_F=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m_0}(3\pi^2n)^{2/3}\), and evaluate \(E_F\) for copper, \(n\approx8.5\times10^{28}\ \text{m}^{-3}\).

Show Solution

Integrating \(g_c(E)=\frac{1}{2\pi^2}(2m_0/\hbar^2)^{3/2}\sqrt{E}\) from 0 to \(E_F\) gives \(n=\frac{1}{3\pi^2}(2m_0E_F/\hbar^2)^{3/2}\); solving for \(E_F\) gives \(E_F=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0}(3\pi^2n)^{2/3}\). For copper: \(3\pi^2n\approx2.52\times10^{30}\ \text{m}^{-3}, so \((3\pi^2n)^{2/3}\approx1.83\times10^{20}\ \text{m}^{-2}\), and \(E_F=\frac{(1.055\times10^{-34})^2}{2(9.11\times10^{-31})}(1.83\times10^{20})\approx1.11\times10^{-18}\ \text{J}\approx6.9\ \text{eV}, close to copper's textbook Fermi energy of about 7 eV.

docs.title: Problem 19
docs.text:
A semiconductor's conduction band actually has two equivalent "valleys" (band minima at symmetry-related k-points) rather than one, each with the same effective mass. Explain, qualitatively, how this changes the total conduction-band density of states compared to a single-valley model with the same per-valley effective mass, and why real silicon's conduction band (which has six equivalent valleys) requires this correction.

Show Solution

Each equivalent valley independently contributes its own set of parabolic states near the conduction-band edge, so the total density of states is simply the single-valley result multiplied by the number of equivalent valleys, \(g_c^{\text{total}}(E) = M_c\,g_c^{\text{single valley}}(E)\). Real silicon's conduction band has \(M_c=6\) equivalent valleys along the \(\langle100\rangle\) directions, so any quantitative carrier-concentration calculation (Chapters 9-10) must include this valley-degeneracy factor rather than using the single-valley formula alone.

docs.title: Problem 20
docs.text:
A hypothetical semiconductor has \(E_g=1.5\) eV, an electron effective mass \(m_e^*=0.09\,m_0\), and is direct-gap. (a) Find the threshold wavelength for direct optical absorption. (b) If the conduction-band curvature were instead four times smaller (larger effective mass), how would the density of states near the band edge change? (c) Would this material be classified as a semiconductor or an insulator, and why?

Show Solution

(a) \(\lambda=hc/E_g=(4.136\times10^{-15})(3.0\times10^8)/1.5 \approx 8.3\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}=830\ \text{nm}. (b) A curvature four times smaller means an effective mass four times larger (\(m^*\propto1/\text{curvature}\)), and since \(g_c(E)\propto(m^*)^{3/2}\), the density of states near the band edge would increase by a factor of \(4^{1.5}=8\). (c) With \(E_g=1.5\) eV — a completely full valence band and empty conduction band separated by a gap well under the roughly 4 eV insulator threshold — this material is a semiconductor, comparable to real materials like GaAs (1.42 eV) and CdTe (1.5 eV).

docs.title: Chapter 6 Quiz - Band Structure and the Fermi Level
Quiz: Band Structure and the Fermi Level
docs.text:
Test your understanding of band structure, effective mass, density of states, and the Fermi level covered in Chapter 6 with these 20 questions.

Question 1

What defines a direct bandgap material?

  1. The conduction-band minimum and valence-band maximum occur at the same crystal momentum k
  2. The conduction-band minimum and valence-band maximum occur at different crystal momenta
  3. The material has no band gap at all
  4. The material conducts electricity like a metal
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

A direct bandgap material has its conduction-band minimum and valence-band maximum at the same crystal momentum k, allowing a photon alone to drive a vertical band-edge transition.

Concept Tested: Direct Bandgap

Question 2

Which of these materials is an indirect bandgap material?

  1. GaAs
  2. InP
  3. Silicon
  4. All of the above are direct-gap
Show Answer

Correct Answer: C

Silicon's conduction-band minimum sits away from k=0 (near the Brillouin zone's X point) while its valence-band maximum sits at k=0, making it indirect. GaAs and InP are both direct-gap III-V compounds.

Concept Tested: Indirect Bandgap

Question 3

Why must a photon-driven band-to-band transition be nearly vertical on an E-k diagram?

  1. Because a photon carries negligible crystal momentum compared to typical electron crystal momenta
  2. Because photons cannot interact with electrons at all
  3. Because vertical transitions have zero energy
  4. Because E-k diagrams only allow vertical lines to be drawn
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

A photon's momentum, hc/λ, is roughly three orders of magnitude smaller than typical crystal momenta, so conservation of crystal momentum forces a photon-only transition to have Δk ≈ 0 — a vertical line on the E-k diagram.

Concept Tested: E-K Diagram

Question 4

What extra particle does an indirect band-to-band transition require, beyond a photon?

  1. A second photon
  2. A phonon, to supply the missing crystal momentum
  3. A neutrino
  4. Nothing — indirect transitions need only a photon
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Because the band edges are offset in k, a phonon (a quantum of lattice vibration) must supply or absorb the crystal momentum difference Δk, making indirect transitions intrinsically less probable than direct ones.

Concept Tested: Indirect Bandgap

Question 5

How is effective mass \(m^*\) defined?

  1. \(m^* = \hbar^2/(d^2E/dk^2)\), from the curvature of a band at an extremum
  2. \(m^* = E/c^2\)
  3. \(m^*\) is always equal to the free-electron mass \(m_0\)
  4. \(m^* = \hbar k\)
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

Effective mass is defined from a band's curvature at an extremum, \(1/m^*=(1/\hbar^2)\,d^2E/dk^2\), letting electrons there be treated with ordinary Newtonian mechanics.

Concept Tested: Effective Mass

Question 6

A band curves very sharply near its minimum (large \(d^2E/dk^2\)). What does this imply about the effective mass there?

  1. The effective mass is large
  2. The effective mass is small
  3. Curvature has no relation to effective mass
  4. The effective mass is negative
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Since \(m^*=\hbar^2/(d^2E/dk^2)\), effective mass is inversely proportional to curvature — a sharply-curved band gives a small effective mass, as in GaAs's conduction band.

Concept Tested: Effective Mass

Question 7

What is the practical benefit of defining effective mass?

  1. It lets electrons and holes near a band extremum be treated with ordinary Newtonian mechanics, \(F=m^*a\)
  2. It eliminates the need for the Schrödinger equation entirely, at all energies
  3. It proves that electrons have no mass
  4. It only applies to free particles, not electrons in crystals
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

Effective mass hides the complicated periodic-potential band structure inside one number, letting an electron near a band extremum respond to forces exactly like a classical free particle of mass \(m^*\).

Concept Tested: Effective Mass

Question 8

What does the density of states \(g(E)\) represent?

  1. The number of allowed electron states per unit volume per unit energy
  2. The probability that a state is occupied
  3. The total number of electrons in a crystal
  4. The band gap energy
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

\(g(E)\,dE\) is the number of allowed electron states per unit volume with energy between E and E+dE — it says nothing about occupation, only availability.

Concept Tested: Density of States

Question 9

How does the conduction-band density of states \(g_c(E)\) depend on energy above the band edge, for a parabolic band?

  1. It is constant, independent of energy
  2. It grows linearly with energy
  3. It grows as the square root of energy above the band edge
  4. It decreases as energy increases
Show Answer

Correct Answer: C

\(g_c(E)=\frac{1}{2\pi^2}(2m_e^*/\hbar^2)^{3/2}\sqrt{E-E_c}\) — a direct result of counting states in three-dimensional k-space, growing as the square root of energy above \(E_c\).

Concept Tested: Density of States

Question 10

What is the Fermi-Dirac distribution \(f(E)\)?

  1. The number of states at energy E
  2. The probability that a state of energy E is occupied by an electron
  3. The band gap energy
  4. The effective mass of an electron at energy E
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

\(f(E)=1/[1+\exp((E-E_F)/k_BT)]\) gives the probability that a state of energy E is occupied, parameterized by the Fermi level \(E_F\).

Concept Tested: Fermi Level

Question 11

What is \(f(E)\) exactly at \(E=E_F\), for any temperature \(T>0\)?

  1. 0
  2. 1
  3. 1/2
  4. Undefined
Show Answer

Correct Answer: C

Setting \(E=E_F\) makes the exponential term equal 1, so \(f(E_F)=1/(1+1)=1/2\) — the Fermi level is, by definition, the energy at which occupation probability is exactly one-half.

Concept Tested: Fermi Level

Question 12

What happens to the Fermi-Dirac distribution as \(T\to0\)?

  1. It becomes a sharp step function, 1 below \(E_F\) and 0 above it
  2. It becomes completely flat at 1/2 everywhere
  3. It becomes undefined
  4. It oscillates rapidly
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

As T→0 the exponential becomes infinitely steep, collapsing \(f(E)\) into a step function; the step's location, the highest occupied state, is called the Fermi energy.

Concept Tested: Fermi Energy

Question 13

How does "Fermi level" differ from "Fermi energy" as used in this chapter?

  1. They are completely unrelated quantities
  2. Fermi level is the general parameter \(E_F\) at any temperature; Fermi energy is specifically its T=0 value
  3. Fermi energy applies only to insulators; Fermi level applies only to metals
  4. Fermi level is always exactly zero
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Fermi level is the general Fermi-Dirac parameter at any temperature (and can lie inside a gap); Fermi energy is specifically the T=0 value, equal to the energy of the highest occupied state.

Concept Tested: Fermi Energy

Question 14

In an intrinsic semiconductor, the Fermi level sits inside the band gap, where \(g(E)=0\). Is this a contradiction?

  1. Yes, the Fermi level must always sit exactly on a real occupied state
  2. No, the Fermi level is a mathematical parameter and does not require a real state at that exact energy
  3. Yes, this means the semiconductor has no electrons at all
  4. No, because semiconductors have no density of states anywhere
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

The Fermi level only needs to correctly set the tails of \(f(E)\) reaching into the conduction and valence bands; it does not require an actual occupied state to sit exactly at \(E_F\).

Concept Tested: Fermi Level

Question 15

What band-structure condition defines a metal?

  1. A large band gap with the Fermi level exactly in the middle
  2. The Fermi level lies inside a partially-filled band, or bands overlap in energy
  3. All electron states are completely full
  4. The material has no electrons at all
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

A metal has its Fermi level inside a band that is only partially filled (or has overlapping bands), so empty states sit immediately adjacent in energy to filled ones, allowing easy conduction.

Concept Tested: Metal Band Structure

Question 16

What is the key difference between an insulator's band structure and a semiconductor's?

  1. Insulators have a partially-filled band; semiconductors do not
  2. They are qualitatively identical (full valence band, empty conduction band) but differ in band gap size
  3. Semiconductors have no band gap at all
  4. Insulators have overlapping bands; semiconductors do not
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Both have a completely full valence band and empty conduction band at T=0; an insulator's gap (roughly >4 eV) is too large for meaningful thermal excitation, while a semiconductor's smaller gap (roughly 0.1-3 eV) allows technologically useful thermal excitation at room temperature.

Concept Tested: Insulator Band Structure

Question 17

What defines a semimetal band structure?

  1. A very large band gap, over 4 eV
  2. Bands that touch or slightly overlap, with very little density of states at the overlap energy
  3. A completely empty valence band
  4. Identical band structure to a typical metal, with no differences
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

A semimetal's bands touch or slightly overlap, but with very low density of states right at the overlap energy, giving a much lower carrier density than a true metal — bismuth and graphite are examples.

Concept Tested: Semimetal

Question 18

Magnesium has two valence electrons per atom, which naive electron counting suggests should exactly fill one band (making it an insulator), yet magnesium conducts well. Why?

  1. Magnesium has no band gap theory applicable to it
  2. Its valence and conduction bands overlap in energy, leaving both partially filled and the Fermi level inside a band
  3. Magnesium is actually an insulator in reality
  4. Magnesium has an unusually large band gap
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

Because magnesium's bands overlap in energy rather than being separated by a gap, electrons partially populate both bands, leaving the Fermi level inside a partially-filled band — the metal band structure condition, despite the simple electron-counting argument.

Concept Tested: Metal Band Structure

Question 19

Why are GaAs-based devices much more efficient LEDs and laser diodes than silicon-based devices?

  1. GaAs has a larger band gap than silicon
  2. GaAs is direct-gap, so a photon alone can drive band-edge emission, while silicon's indirect gap requires a much less probable phonon-assisted process
  3. Silicon has no conduction band
  4. GaAs has a smaller effective mass, which is unrelated to light emission
Show Answer

Correct Answer: B

GaAs's direct gap allows efficient photon-only recombination at the band edge, while silicon's indirect gap requires a much rarer phonon-assisted process, making silicon a poor light emitter despite being an excellent solar-cell absorber.

Concept Tested: Direct Bandgap

Question 20

Which two questions, according to this chapter, are sufficient to classify a material as a metal, insulator, semiconductor, or semimetal?

  1. Is the highest occupied band partially filled (or do bands overlap), and if not, how large is the band gap?
  2. What is the material's color, and how heavy are its atoms?
  3. Is the material direct-gap or indirect-gap?
  4. What is the material's effective mass only?
Show Answer

Correct Answer: A

Whether the highest band is partially filled (or bands overlap) separates metals from the rest; among materials with a real gap, the gap's size separates insulators from semiconductors, and near-zero-gap materials with low density of states at the overlap are semimetals.

Concept Tested: Semiconductor Band Structure

docs.title: Learning Graph for Semiconductor Physics
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long. This course has 218 concepts spanning prerequisite mathematics and electromagnetics, crystal structure, quantum mechanics and band theory, carrier statistics and transport, the p-n junction, and semiconductor devices. Concepts 201–218 (algebra, trigonometry, complex numbers, differentiation, integration, partial derivatives, vectors, gradient, divergence, curl, electric flux, Gauss's Law, SI units, and fundamental constants) were added after Chapter 1 was written, to represent the prerequisite mathematics and electromagnetics it actually teaches. They were appended with new IDs rather than inserted at the front, so that every original concept ID (1–200) is preserved.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
This taxonomy organizes the 218 concepts in the Semiconductor Physics learning graph into 12 categories, each evenly distributed to avoid any single category dominating the graph.

Category TaxonomyID Description Physics & Math Foundations FOUND Prerequisite physics, mathematics, and quantum mechanics concepts (mechanics, electrostatics, algebra, trigonometry, complex numbers, calculus, vector calculus, Gauss's Law, thermal physics, wave-particle duality, the Schrödinger equation) that underlie the rest of the course. Crystal Structure & Bonding CRYS Crystalline solids: lattice types, unit cells, Miller indices, and the bonding that holds semiconductor crystals together. Quantum Mechanics & Band Theory QMBT How periodic crystal potentials give rise to energy bands, band gaps, and the E-k relationships that distinguish metals, insulators, and semiconductors. Semiconductor Materials & Doping MATL Intrinsic vs. extrinsic materials, donor/acceptor doping, ionization, and the temperature regimes of doped semiconductors. Carrier Statistics STAT Fermi-Dirac statistics, density of states, and the equations governing electron and hole concentrations at equilibrium. Carrier Transport TRAN Drift and diffusion current, mobility, scattering, conductivity, and related transport phenomena (Hall effect, Einstein relation). Non-Equilibrium Carriers NEQ Excess carrier generation and recombination mechanisms, carrier lifetime, and the continuity equation governing non-equilibrium carrier profiles. P-N Junction PNJ The physics of the p-n junction: depletion region, built-in potential, capacitance, the ideal diode equation, and breakdown mechanisms. Metal-Semiconductor Junctions MSJ Schottky barriers, ohmic contacts, and the physics of metal-semiconductor interfaces. MOS Capacitor & Surfaces MOS The MOS capacitor structure, surface conditions (accumulation, depletion, inversion), and threshold voltage — the physical basis of the MOSFET. Optical & Thermal Properties OPT Light absorption, photogeneration, and the optoelectronic and thermal properties of semiconductors. Devices & Applications DEV Applied device concepts (diodes, transistors, device modeling) and the capstone project connecting physics to real device performance.

  • Non-circularity: No definition references a term that is itself undefined in this glossary or in a lower-numbered prerequisite concept. Dependency order from the learning graph (e.g., Vectors → Gradient → Divergence/Curl → Gauss's Law) was used to check that each definition only relies on already-defined, simpler terms.
