docs.title: Bonding and Crystal Order Explorer
docs.text:
Bonding and Crystal Order Explorer

← Back to Chapter 4: Chemical Bonding in Semiconductor Crystals

Description

This MicroSim has two linked views, selected by a top-level dropdown. The Bond Types view schematically compares covalent bonding (a shared electron pair between two atoms), ionic bonding (an electron transferred completely between a cation and an anion, held together by Coulomb attraction), and metallic bonding (valence electrons delocalized into a mobile "electron sea" surrounding fixed positive ion cores). The Crystal Order view compares a perfectly periodic single crystal, a polycrystalline mosaic of small, differently-oriented grains separated by grain boundaries, and an amorphous arrangement with no long-range order at all — with an optional toggle that overlays vacancy, interstitial, and substitutional point defects onto the single-crystal grid.

Key Features

  • ● Two linked views in one tool: Bond Types and Crystal Order
  • ● Covalent, ionic, and metallic bonding drawn schematically with electron behavior visually distinguished
  • ● Single crystal, polycrystalline, and amorphous order compared directly, with rotated per-grain grids in Polycrystalline mode
  • ● Toggleable point defects (vacancy, interstitial, substitutional) with an on-canvas legend
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window
How to Use
  1. Select "Bond Types" and cycle through Covalent, Ionic, and Metallic
  2. Switch to "Crystal Order" and cycle through Single Crystal, Polycrystalline, and Amorphous
  3. In Single Crystal mode, check "Show defects" and use the legend to identify the vacancy, interstitial, and substitutional markers
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Analyze (L2-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Compare, Classify, Explain

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Distinguish covalent, ionic, and metallic bonding by their electron behavior
  • ✓ Compare long-range order across single-crystal, polycrystalline, and amorphous arrangements
  • ✓ Classify a described crystal irregularity as a vacancy, interstitial, or substitutional defect
References
  • ● Chemical Bond — Wikipedia
  • ● Crystallographic Defect — Wikipedia
  • ● Amorphous Solid — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 4: Chemical Bonding in Semiconductor Crystals — this textbook

docs.title: Coulomb's Law Force and Field Explorer
docs.text:
Coulomb's Law Force and Field Explorer

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim lets students adjust two point charges (\(q_1\), \(q_2\)) and their separation (\(r\)) and immediately see the resulting electrostatic force \(F\), the electric field \(E\) and potential \(V\) that \(q_1\) creates at \(q_2\)'s location, and the electrostatic potential energy \(U\) of the pair — all computed from real SI values using \(k=8.99\times10^9\ \text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2\).

Key Features

  • ● Three independent sliders for \(q_1\), \(q_2\) (−5 to +5 nC), and separation \(r\) (0.2 to 5 nm)
  • ● Live numeric readouts of force, field, potential, and energy in scientific notation
  • ● Log-scaled force arrows so both very small and very large forces remain visible on screen
  • ● Reset button returning to the default \(q_1=+2\) nC, \(q_2=-1\) nC, \(r=1\) nm
How to Use
  1. Drag the \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) sliders to change charge magnitude and sign
  2. Drag the \(r\) slider to change separation and watch \(F\) change much faster than \(E\) or \(V\)
  3. Read the numeric panel to see the exact computed values in SI units
  4. Click Reset to return to the default configuration
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Apply Coulomb's Law to compute the force between two point charges
  • ✓ Apply the point-charge field and potential equations to compute \(E\) and \(V\)
  • ✓ Verify, by direct manipulation, that force falls off faster with distance (\(1/r^2\)) than potential does (\(1/r\))
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the boxed Coulomb's Law, field, and potential equations from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict what happens to \(F\) if \(r\) is doubled
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Set \(q_1=q_2=2\) nC and record \(F\), \(E\), \(V\), \(U\) at \(r=1\) nm
  2. Double \(r\) to 2 nm and compare the new readouts against the prediction (\(F\) should drop to 1/4, \(V\) to 1/2)
  3. Flip the sign of \(q_2\) and observe the arrows reverse direction and \(U\) become negative
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Compare results with Worked Example 9 in the chapter
  • ● Discuss why this distinction matters for the depletion-region field in Chapter 14
References
  • ● Coulomb's Law — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 1: Coulomb's Law — this textbook

docs.title: Coulomb's Law Force Vectors
docs.text:
Coulomb's Law Force Vectors

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim shows two point charges, \(q_1\) and \(q_2\), drawn along a horizontal line with force vectors indicating the direction of the electrostatic force each charge exerts on the other. Selecting a charge combination toggles between repulsive (like-charge) and attractive (unlike-charge) configurations, and a separation slider shows how the relative force magnitude changes with distance.

Key Features

  • ● Three charge combinations: like-positive, like-negative, and unlike charges
  • ● Force vectors drawn along the line connecting the two charges, pointing apart (repulsion) or together (attraction)
  • ● Separation slider showing the relative force magnitude scale with distance (arrow length shrinks as \(r\) grows)
  • ● Color-coded charges: red for positive, blue for negative
How to Use
  1. Select a charge combination from the dropdown to compare like and unlike charges
  2. Drag the separation slider to see how the force arrows shrink as the charges move apart
  3. Observe the direction of the force vectors and the attractive/repulsive label below the charges
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand (L2)  |  Bloom Verb: Illustrate

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Explain that the electrostatic force is a vector directed along the line connecting two point charges
  • ✓ Predict whether a pair of charges will attract or repel based on their signs
  • ✓ Recognize that force magnitude falls off quickly (inverse-square) as separation increases
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Introduce Coulomb's Law in words before showing the equation
  • ● Ask students to predict what happens when two positive charges are brought close together
During the Simulation (5 minutes)
  1. Switch between all three charge combinations and note the arrow directions
  2. Slide the separation control from minimum to maximum and watch the arrows shrink
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Connect the diagram to the boxed Coulomb's Law equation in the chapter
  • ● Preview that the next MicroSim (Coulomb's Law Force and Field Explorer) computes the actual numeric force
References
  • ● Coulomb's Law — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 1: Coulomb's Law — this textbook

docs.title: Crystal Structure Explorer
docs.text:
Crystal Structure Explorer

← Back to Chapter 3: Crystal Lattices and Structures

Description

This MicroSim renders a fully rotatable, pannable, and zoomable 3D model of one conventional unit cell for each of the nine crystal structures most important to solid-state and semiconductor physics: Simple Cubic (SC), Body-Centered Cubic (BCC), Face-Centered Cubic (FCC), Hexagonal Close-Packed (HCP), Diamond Cubic, Zinc Blende, Rock Salt (NaCl), Cesium Chloride (CsCl), and Wurtzite. A dropdown switches between structures; atoms are drawn at their correct fractional positions with correct sharing/coordination, compound structures use a distinct color per species with a legend, and a live readout panel reports crystal system, Bravais lattice and basis, atoms per conventional cell, coordination number, nearest-neighbor distance, atomic packing factor, example materials, and semiconductor relevance for whichever structure is selected.

This tool was expanded from an earlier "Cubic Lattice Explorer" that covered only SC, BCC, and FCC. Because HCP and the two hexagonal-family structures (Wurtzite) are not cubic, the tool and its title were generalized to Crystal Structure Explorer to accurately describe its full scope.

Key Features

  • ● Nine structures in one tool: SC, BCC, FCC, HCP, Diamond Cubic, Zinc Blende, Rock Salt, CsCl, and Wurtzite
  • ● Free 3D orbit, pan, and zoom via p5.js \(\texttt{orbitControl()}\) — left-drag to rotate, right-drag to pan, scroll to zoom
  • ● Color-coded species with a legend for every compound structure (Zinc Blende, Rock Salt, CsCl, Wurtzite)
  • ● Toggleable atom labels, unit-cell edges, nearest-neighbor bonds, and primitive-vs-conventional cell so students can isolate exactly one variable at a time
  • ● Adjustable atom size and a Reset Camera button
  • ● Miller-index plane (h k l) and direction [u v w] overlay for the six cubic structures
  • ● Fullscreen mode for closer inspection on smaller screens
  • ● Live readout panel reporting crystal system, Bravais lattice/basis, atoms per cell, coordination number, nearest-neighbor distance, packing factor, examples, and semiconductor relevance
Structure Reference Table

All lattice-parameter relationships below use \(a\) for the cubic lattice constant and \(c\) for the hexagonal out-of-plane constant (ideal \(c/a=\sqrt{8/3}\approx1.633\)).

Structure Crystal system Bravais lattice + basis Atoms/cell Coord. number Nearest-neighbor distance Packing factor Example materials Simple Cubic (SC) Cubic Simple cubic (P); 1 atom at (0,0,0) 1 6 \(a\) 0.524 Polonium Body-Centered Cubic (BCC) Cubic Body-centered cubic (I); (0,0,0) + (½,½,½) 2 8 \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}a\) 0.680 α-Fe, Cr, W, Na Face-Centered Cubic (FCC) Cubic Face-centered cubic (F); (0,0,0) + 3 face centers 4 12 \(\tfrac{a}{\sqrt2}\) 0.740 Al, Cu, Au, Ag Hexagonal Close-Packed (HCP) Hexagonal Simple hexagonal + 2-atom basis, ABAB stacking 6 12 \(a\) 0.740 Mg, Zn, Ti, Co, Be Diamond Cubic Cubic FCC + 2-atom basis (0,0,0), (¼,¼,¼), same element 8 4 \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}a\) 0.340 Si (a=0.543 nm), Ge (a=0.566 nm), C Zinc Blende Cubic FCC + 2-atom basis (0,0,0), (¼,¼,¼), two species 8 4 \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}a\) varies with ionic/atomic radii GaAs (a=0.565 nm), GaP, InP, InAs, ZnS Rock Salt (NaCl) Cubic Two interpenetrating FCC lattices offset by (½,0,0)a 8 6 \(\tfrac{a}{2}\) varies with ionic radii NaCl, MgO Cesium Chloride (CsCl) Cubic Simple cubic (P) + 2-atom basis (0,0,0), (½,½,½), two species 2 8 \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}a\) varies with ionic radii CsCl, CsBr, CsI Wurtzite Hexagonal Two HCP-type sublattices offset along c by u (ideal u=3/8), two species 12 4 \(u\cdot c \approx 0.612a\) varies with ionic/atomic radii GaN, AlN, ZnO, CdS

Special Focus: Diamond Cubic and Zinc Blende

These two structures are geometrically identical — both are built from two interpenetrating FCC sublattices offset by \((1/4,1/4,1/4)a\) along the body diagonal, giving every atom exactly 4 nearest neighbors arranged tetrahedrally (coordination number 4, far lower than the 12 of a simple FCC lattice). The only difference is chemistry:

  • ● Diamond Cubic places the same element on both sublattices. Silicon and germanium — the two workhorse elemental semiconductors — both crystallize this way, with covalent Si–Si or Ge–Ge bonds arranged tetrahedrally.
  • ● Zinc Blende places two different elements, one per sublattice. GaAs is the canonical example — most III–V compound semiconductors (GaAs, GaP, InP, InAs) used in LEDs, laser diodes, solar cells, and high-frequency transistors adopt this structure. The two-species arrangement breaks the inversion symmetry that pure Diamond Cubic has, which is why compound semiconductors can be piezoelectric while silicon and germanium cannot.
How to Use
  1. Choose a structure from the Crystal structure dropdown (9 options, grouped from simplest to most complex)
  2. Left-click and drag to orbit the structure; right-click and drag to pan; scroll or pinch to zoom
  3. Toggle atom labels, unit-cell edges, nearest-neighbor bonds, and the primitive-cell overlay to isolate what you want to inspect
  4. Enable the plane/direction overlay and enter Miller indices (h k l) or a direction [u v w] to see crystallographic planes and directions for the cubic structures
  5. Use Reset Camera to return to the default view, or the fullscreen button (top-right of the canvas) to enlarge the whole tool
  6. Read the panel below the canvas for crystal system, Bravais lattice/basis, atoms per cell, coordination number, nearest-neighbor distance, packing factor, examples, and semiconductor relevance
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Apply / Analyze (L2-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Identify, Calculate, Compare, Explain

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Identify the atom positions that define all nine major crystal structures used in solid-state and semiconductor physics
  • ✓ Calculate atoms per unit cell using corner, face, edge, and body-center sharing fractions
  • ✓ Compare coordination number and atomic packing factor across cubic, hexagonal, and compound structures
  • ✓ Explain why Silicon and Germanium adopt Diamond Cubic while III–V compounds such as GaAs adopt the geometrically identical Zinc Blende structure
  • ✓ Distinguish a true Bravais lattice from a lattice-plus-basis description, using CsCl (Simple Cubic + 2-atom basis, not BCC) as a concrete counterexample
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review unit cell, lattice constant, basis, and coordination number from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict which structures pack atoms most and least efficiently
During the Simulation (15 minutes)
  1. Cycle through SC → BCC → FCC → HCP and record atoms/cell, coordination number, and packing factor for each
  2. Switch to Diamond Cubic, enable bonds, and count the 4 tetrahedral bonds leaving an interior atom; compare to FCC's coordination of 12
  3. Switch to Zinc Blende and observe that every bond connects a blue and an orange atom, never two of the same color
  4. Compare Rock Salt (CN=6, octahedral) and CsCl (CN=8, cubic) to Zinc Blende (CN=4, tetrahedral) to see how coordination geometry differs by structure
  5. Switch to Wurtzite (GaN) and compare its two-sublattice hexagonal geometry to plain HCP
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Have students derive the packing-fraction formulas for SC, BCC, and FCC on paper and compare to the readout values
  • ● Discuss why silicon (Diamond Cubic) and GaAs (Zinc Blende) share identical geometry but different electrical and optical properties, previewing the covalent-bonding discussion in Chapter 4
References
  • ● Cubic Crystal System — Wikipedia
  • ● Close-Packing of Equal Spheres — Wikipedia
  • ● Diamond Cubic Crystal Structure — Wikipedia
  • ● Zinc Blende Crystal Structure — Wikipedia
  • ● Rock Salt (NaCl) Structure — Wikipedia
  • ● Wurtzite Crystal Structure — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 3: Crystal Lattices and Structures — this textbook

docs.title: de Broglie Wavelength Explorer
docs.text:
de Broglie Wavelength Explorer

← Back to Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations

Description

This MicroSim lets students choose an object — electron, proton, neutron, baseball, bowling ball, or a custom mass — and a velocity, then computes its de Broglie wavelength \(\lambda = h/(mv)\) using \(h = 6.626\times10^{-34}\) J·s. A log-scale ruler plots the computed wavelength alongside reference lengths (atomic diameter, visible-light wavelength, red blood cell diameter) to make it visually obvious that matter waves only matter at quantum scales.

Key Features

  • ● Object dropdown with electron, proton, neutron, baseball, bowling ball, and custom mass presets
  • ● Custom mass slider on a log10 scale spanning subatomic to macroscopic masses
  • ● Velocity slider from 0 to \(10^7\) m/s (non-relativistic range)
  • ● Log-scale ruler comparing the computed wavelength to atomic diameter, visible light, and a red blood cell
  • ● Three preset buttons for a fast electron, a thermal neutron, and a thrown baseball
How to Use
  1. Choose an object from the dropdown, or select "Custom" to unlock the mass slider
  2. Drag the velocity slider and watch the wavelength readout and ruler marker respond
  3. Click a preset button to jump to a worked-example configuration
  4. Compare the red marker to the green reference lines to judge whether the wavelength is quantum-scale or immeasurably small
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Apply \(\lambda = h/(mv)\) to compute the de Broglie wavelength of any object
  • ✓ Compare wavelengths across many orders of magnitude using a log-scale ruler
  • ✓ Explain why matter waves are observable for electrons and neutrons but not for macroscopic objects
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the boxed de Broglie relation \(\lambda = h/(mv)\) from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict whether a thrown baseball has a measurable wavelength
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Click "Electron at 1e7 m/s" and record where the marker lands relative to the atomic-diameter reference
  2. Click "Thermal neutron" and compare its wavelength to the electron's
  3. Click "Baseball" and confirm the marker falls completely off the left edge of the ruler
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Discuss why electron diffraction experiments use crystal lattices as a "diffraction grating"
  • ● Connect this scale argument to why quantum effects dominate carrier transport in semiconductors later in the course
References
  • ● Matter Wave (de Broglie Wavelength) — Wikipedia
  • ● Wave-Particle Duality — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations — this textbook

docs.title: Density of States and Fermi Level Explorer
docs.text:
Density of States and Fermi Level Explorer

← Back to Chapter 6: Band Structure and the Fermi Level

Description

This MicroSim draws a valence-like density of states \(g_v(E)\propto\sqrt{E_v-E}\) and a conduction-like density of states \(g_c(E)\propto\sqrt{E-E_c}\) side by side with a matching band-occupation bar, for four presets: Metal and Semimetal (where the two bands overlap in energy) and Semiconductor and Insulator (where they are separated by a real gap of different sizes). Both panels are shaded by the Fermi-Dirac occupation probability \(f(E)=1/[1+\exp((E-E_F)/k_BT)]\), so dragging the thermal energy slider visibly smears the sharp T=0 occupied/empty boundary near the dashed Fermi level line.

Key Features

  • ● Four material presets: Metal, Insulator, Semiconductor, Semimetal, all built from the same underlying model
  • ● Linked band-occupation and density-of-states panels sharing the same energy axis
  • ● Live Fermi-Dirac shading showing occupied vs. available states at any temperature
  • ● Adjustable thermal energy kT to visualize smearing of the T=0 step
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window
How to Use
  1. Select "Insulator" and confirm E_F sits in a wide white (empty) gap between the green and blue bands
  2. Switch to "Semiconductor" and compare the much narrower gap, with E_F still inside it
  3. Switch to "Metal" then "Semimetal" and compare how much density of states exists right at E_F in each case
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Analyze (L2-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Interpret, Compare, Classify

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Interpret a density-of-states curve and identify where it is zero versus nonzero
  • ✓ Compare Fermi-level position relative to the bands across metal, insulator, semiconductor, and semimetal presets
  • ✓ Classify a material from its band-structure and Fermi-level picture alone
References
  • ● Density of States — Wikipedia
  • ● Fermi Level — Wikipedia
  • ● Semimetal — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 6: Band Structure and the Fermi Level — this textbook

docs.title: Diamond / Zincblende Structure Explorer
docs.text:
Diamond / Zincblende Structure Explorer

← Back to Chapter 3: Crystal Lattices and Structures

Description

This MicroSim renders the diamond-cubic conventional unit cell as two interpenetrating Face-Centered Cubic sublattices — one at the corners and face centers, the other offset by \((\tfrac14,\tfrac14,\tfrac14)a\) along the body diagonal — connected by the four tetrahedral bonds that give every atom coordination number 4. Students click and drag to orbit the structure and toggle between Diamond mode (a single element, such as silicon) and Zincblende mode (two elements, such as gallium and arsenide, distinguished by color).

Key Features

  • ● Free 3D rotation via p5.js \(\texttt{orbitControl()}\) — click-drag to spin, scroll to zoom
  • ● Diamond / Zincblende toggle switching between single-species and two-species coloring with a legend
  • ● 16 tetrahedral bonds drawn between each of the 4 interior atoms and its 4 nearest neighbors
  • ● Live readout panel reporting atoms per cell (8) and coordination number (4)
How to Use
  1. Choose a mode from the Structure dropdown (Diamond or Zincblende)
  2. Click and drag anywhere on the 3D view to rotate the unit cell
  3. Scroll or pinch to zoom in and trace individual bonds
  4. Read the panel below the canvas for atoms per cell, coordination number, and the color legend
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand (L2)  |  Bloom Verb: Describe, Distinguish

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Describe the diamond cubic structure as two interpenetrating FCC sublattices offset along the body diagonal
  • ✓ Distinguish diamond (single-species) from zincblende (two-species) structures despite identical geometry
  • ✓ Explain why tetrahedral bonding gives coordination number 4, lower than close-packed cubic structures
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the Face-Centered Cubic structure from the previous MicroSim and its coordination number of 12
  • ● Ask students to predict why silicon, a semiconductor, might not use a close-packed structure
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. In Diamond mode, rotate the cell and count the 4 bonds leaving one interior atom
  2. Switch to Zincblende mode and verify every bond connects a Ga atom (blue) to an As atom (orange), never the same color to itself
  3. Compare the atoms-per-cell (8) and coordination number (4) readouts to FCC's (4 and 12) from the previous MicroSim
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Discuss why tetrahedral bonding (sp3 hybridization) favors semiconductors like silicon and GaAs
  • ● Preview how Miller indices, covered in the next MicroSim, describe planes cutting through structures like this one
References
  • ● Diamond Cubic Crystal Structure — Wikipedia
  • ● Zincblende Crystal Structure — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 3: Crystal Lattices and Structures — this textbook

docs.title: Direct vs. Indirect Bandgap E-k Explorer
docs.text:
Direct vs. Indirect Bandgap E-k Explorer

← Back to Chapter 6: Band Structure and the Fermi Level

Description

This MicroSim plots simplified valence- and conduction-band parabolas on an E-k diagram, \(E_v(k)=-B_vk^2\) and \(E_c(k)=E_g+a(k-k_0)^2\), for three material presets: direct-gap GaAs (\(k_0=0\)) and indirect-gap Si and Ge (\(k_0\neq0\)). A transition arrow shows either a vertical, photon-only jump at \(k=0\), or a diagonal path split into a vertical photon segment (energy \(E_g\)) and a horizontal phonon segment (momentum \(k_0\)) that together reach the true conduction-band minimum. An effective-mass slider adjusts the conduction band's curvature directly, making the inverse relationship between curvature and effective mass visible.

Key Features

  • ● Three material presets: GaAs (direct), Si (indirect), Ge (indirect), with realistic band gaps
  • ● Switchable transition arrow: vertical (photon only) vs. diagonal (phonon-assisted)
  • ● Adjustable effective mass directly controls conduction-band curvature
  • ● Labeled band extrema mark the valence-band maximum and conduction-band minimum
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window
How to Use
  1. Select "GaAs (Direct)" with "Vertical (photon only)" transition and confirm the arrow lands exactly on the conduction-band minimum
  2. Switch to "Si (Indirect)" and see the same vertical arrow now miss the true minimum, which has shifted to a nonzero k₀
  3. Change Transition to "Diagonal (phonon-assisted)" and confirm the path now reaches the true minimum via a photon segment plus a phonon segment
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Analyze (L2-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Identify, Compare, Analyze

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Identify direct vs. indirect band gaps directly from an E-k diagram
  • ✓ Explain why a photon-only transition can reach the conduction-band minimum only when k₀ = 0
  • ✓ Connect conduction-band curvature to effective mass, and compare curvature across materials
References
  • ● Direct and Indirect Band Gaps — Wikipedia
  • ● Effective Mass — Wikipedia
  • ● Electronic Band Structure — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 6: Band Structure and the Fermi Level — this textbook

docs.title: Electric Field and Flux Explorer
docs.text:
Electric Field and Flux Explorer

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim shows the radial electric field of a point charge together with a small flat test surface placed a fixed distance away. A slider tilts the surface's normal vector relative to the field, and a live readout shows the electric field magnitude, the surface area, and the resulting flux \(\Phi_E = EA\cos\theta\) — including the special cases of maximum flux (\(\theta=0°\), normal aligned with the field) and zero flux (\(\theta=90°\), surface parallel to the field).

Key Features

  • ● Charge slider (−5 to +5 nC) that reverses the field direction and the color of the radiating arrows
  • ● Distance slider moving the test surface closer to or farther from the charge
  • ● Angle slider (0–90°) tilting the surface's normal vector relative to the field
  • ● Live numeric readout of \(E\), \(\cos\theta\), and \(\Phi_E\)
How to Use
  1. Set the angle slider to 0° and note the flux is at its maximum (normal aligned with the field)
  2. Slide the angle to 90° and note the flux drops to exactly zero
  3. Change the distance slider and observe that \(E\) changes but \(\Phi_E\) still scales the same way with \(\cos\theta\)
  4. Flip the charge sign to see the field arrows reverse direction
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Compute the electric field of a point charge at a given distance
  • ✓ Apply \(\Phi_E = EA\cos\theta\) to compute electric flux through a flat surface
  • ✓ Explain why flux is maximized when a surface is perpendicular to the field and zero when parallel to it
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the definition of electric flux from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict the flux at θ=45°
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Sweep the angle slider from 0° to 90° and record the flux at 0°, 45°, and 90°
  2. Verify the 45° value matches \(E \cdot A \cdot \cos(45°)\) computed by hand
  3. Move the surface closer to the charge and note how much faster \(E\) grows than a linear change
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Preview the next MicroSim (Gauss's Law Explorer), which shows what happens when a surface completely encloses the charge
  • ● Discuss why a solar cell's tilt angle relative to the sun affects the light flux it captures, as a real-world analogy
References
  • ● Electric Flux — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 1: Electric Flux — this textbook

docs.title: Electron Configuration Explorer
docs.text:
Electron Configuration Explorer

← Back to Chapter 4: Chemical Bonding in Semiconductor Crystals

Description

This MicroSim renders a Bohr-model-style diagram of electron shell filling for any element from hydrogen (Z=1) through argon (Z=18). Electrons are drawn on concentric rings corresponding to their principal shell, filled in standard order (\(1s,\,2s,\,2p,\,3s,\,3p\)), with electrons in the outermost occupied shell — the valence electrons — highlighted in orange and all other (core) electrons in green. A live readout below the diagram reports the full subshell configuration string and the core/valence electron counts, and three preset buttons jump directly to sodium, silicon, and chlorine, the three elements compared in Chapter 4's bonding discussion.

Key Features

  • ● Full Z=1–18 range (hydrogen through argon), covering every element discussed in this chapter
  • ● Core vs. valence color coding (green vs. orange) directly tied to the chapter's bonding explanation
  • ● Live subshell configuration string (e.g. \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^2\)) and core/valence electron counts
  • ● One-click presets for Na, Si, and Cl, the chapter's three worked comparison elements
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window
How to Use
  1. Press "Si (Z=14)" and confirm the configuration string matches the chapter text
  2. Press "Na" and "Cl" and compare their valence electron counts (1 and 7) to silicon's 4
  3. Drag the Z slider slowly across the whole range and watch each shell fill and the outermost ring reset at the start of each new row
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Apply (L2-L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Identify, Compute, Compare

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Determine the electron configuration of any element from Z=1 to 18
  • ✓ Identify the number of core electrons versus valence electrons for a given element
  • ✓ Compare valence electron counts across elements to predict their preferred bonding type
References
  • ● Electron Configuration — Wikipedia
  • ● Valence Electron — Wikipedia
  • ● Bohr Model — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 4: Chemical Bonding in Semiconductor Crystals — this textbook

docs.title: Finite Potential Well Explorer
docs.text:
Finite Potential Well Explorer

← Back to Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations

Description

This MicroSim numerically solves for the bound-state energies of a symmetric finite square well of adjustable width \(L\) and depth \(V_0\), using bisection root-finding on the standard even/odd transcendental matching equations. It plots the well, a dashed energy level for every bound state found, and the selected eigenfunction — clearly showing the wavefunction decaying smoothly into the classically forbidden region outside the well, rather than dropping to exactly zero as it does in the idealized infinite well of Particle in a Box.

Key Features

  • ● Exact bisection solver for finite-well bound states, not an approximation
  • ● Bound-state dropdown that updates automatically as L and V₀ change the available state count
  • ● Infinite-well overlay toggle for a direct side-by-side wavefunction comparison
  • ● Live energy-level ladder with parity (even/odd) labels for every bound state
How to Use
  1. Drag V₀ from minimum to maximum and watch the "Bound states found" count grow
  2. Select each bound state from the dropdown and count its internal nodes
  3. Check "Compare to infinite well" to see the dashed curve forced to zero at the walls versus the solid curve that penetrates them
  4. Adjust L and observe how a wider well packs energy levels more closely together
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply / Analyze (L3-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate, Contrast

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Calculate how the number of bound states depends on well width and depth
  • ✓ Contrast finite-well wavefunction penetration against the infinite well's exact zero at the walls
  • ✓ Identify even vs. odd parity bound states from their wavefunction symmetry
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the "Finite Potential Wells and Barriers" text and the idea of a classically forbidden region
  • ● Ask students to predict whether a shallow, narrow well can always support at least one bound state
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Set V₀ to minimum and confirm exactly one bound state exists, with a visibly leaking wavefunction
  2. Raise V₀ until 3-4 states appear, and record each state's parity and node count
  3. Toggle the infinite-well overlay for the ground state and discuss why the finite-well energy is always somewhat lower
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Connect wavefunction penetration to real confined-carrier devices (quantum wells, doped-atom electrons)
  • ● Preview how generalizing a well to a *barrier* (allowed regions on both sides instead of a well) leads directly into quantum tunneling, covered next
References
  • ● Finite Potential Well — Wikipedia
  • ● Particle in a Box (Infinite Well) — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations — this textbook

docs.title: Gauss's Law Explorer
docs.text:
Gauss's Law Explorer

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim draws a spherical Gaussian surface (shown as a circle, its 2D cross-section) around a point charge. Changing the surface's radius changes the electric field at the surface, but the total flux \(\Phi_E = Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0\) stays exactly the same, since it depends only on the enclosed charge. A toggle button moves the charge outside the surface, showing that flux drops to exactly zero when no charge is enclosed.

Key Features

  • ● Radius slider (1 to 5 nm) that visibly changes the field strength but not the total flux
  • ● Charge slider (−5 to +5 nC) showing flux scales directly with enclosed charge
  • ● Inside/outside toggle demonstrating that flux is exactly zero when the charge is not enclosed
  • ● Live numeric readout of enclosed charge, field at the surface, and total flux
How to Use
  1. Drag the radius slider and watch the flux readout stay fixed while the field readout changes
  2. Drag the charge slider and watch flux scale directly with the enclosed charge
  3. Click "Move Charge Outside Surface" and note the flux immediately drops to zero, regardless of radius
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate, verify

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Apply Gauss's Law to compute total flux from enclosed charge alone
  • ✓ Verify that flux is independent of the Gaussian surface's size or shape
  • ✓ Explain why charge outside a Gaussian surface contributes zero net flux
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review Gauss's Law from the chapter and ask why it is easier to apply than Coulomb's Law for symmetric charge distributions
  • ● Ask students to predict what happens to flux if the radius is doubled
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Double the radius and confirm the flux readout is unchanged while the field readout drops
  2. Double the charge and confirm the flux readout doubles
  3. Move the charge outside and confirm flux reads exactly zero at every radius
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Connect back to Worked Example 10 and Concept Check in the Basic Electromagnetics section
  • ● Preview that Chapter 14 uses this exact technique to find the field inside a p-n junction's depletion region
References
  • ● Gauss's Law — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 1: Gauss's Law — this textbook

docs.title: Gradient, Divergence, and Curl Explorer
docs.text:
Gradient, Divergence, and Curl Explorer

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim lets students switch between the three vector-calculus operators introduced in the chapter — gradient, divergence, and curl — and see each one applied to simple preset fields. In Gradient mode, a colored scalar field (a bowl or a saddle) is overlaid with arrows showing \(\nabla V\), the direction of steepest increase. In Divergence and Curl mode, arrows show a vector field, tinted red/blue (source/sink) or purple (rotational) according to the field's constant analytic divergence or curl.

Key Features

  • ● Operator selector switching between Gradient, Divergence, and Curl
  • ● 2-3 preset fields per operator (bowl/saddle for gradient; source/sink/uniform for divergence; rotational/radial/uniform for curl)
  • ● Quiver-plot arrows at grid points showing field/gradient direction and relative magnitude
  • ● Numeric readout of the exact analytic divergence or curl value for the selected field
How to Use
  1. Choose an operator (Gradient, Divergence, or Curl) from the first dropdown
  2. Choose a preset field from the second dropdown, which updates to show only fields relevant to the selected operator
  3. Compare the arrows and background tint between fields, and read the numeric operator value at the bottom of the canvas
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand (L2)  |  Bloom Verb: Interpret, distinguish

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Distinguish which operator takes a scalar field as input and which take a vector field
  • ✓ Recognize a source field (positive divergence) versus a sink field (negative divergence) versus a divergence-free field
  • ✓ Recognize a rotational field (nonzero curl) versus a curl-free radial or uniform field
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the gradient, divergence, and curl definitions and equations from the chapter
  • ● Ask students which operator they expect to give zero for a uniform field
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. In Gradient mode, compare the bowl and saddle fields and note where the arrows point
  2. In Divergence mode, compare the source and sink fields and note the tint color and sign
  3. In Curl mode, compare the rotational and radial fields and note that only one produces a nonzero curl
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Connect the "Source (outward)" field to Gauss's Law: positive divergence corresponds to positive charge density
  • ● Note that the radial field's zero curl matches the chapter's statement that static electric fields are curl-free
References
  • ● Gradient — Wikipedia
  • ● Divergence — Wikipedia
  • ● Curl — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 1: Vector Calculus — this textbook

docs.title: Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle Explorer
docs.text:
Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle Explorer

← Back to Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations

Description

This MicroSim lets students adjust the position uncertainty \(\Delta x\) of an electron or proton and see the resulting minimum momentum uncertainty \(\Delta p_{min} = \hbar/(2\Delta x)\) and velocity uncertainty \(\Delta v_{min} = \Delta p_{min}/m\), computed from \(\hbar = 1.0546\times10^{-34}\) J·s. Two Gaussian curves — a position wave packet and a momentum spread — visually narrow and widen in opposite directions as the slider moves, making the trade-off in \(\Delta x\,\Delta p \geq \hbar/2\) immediately visible.

Key Features

  • ● Log-scale Δx slider spanning 1 pm to 1 µm
  • ● Particle-type dropdown (electron or proton) converting \(\Delta p\) into \(\Delta v\)
  • ● Two linked Gaussian curves showing the position wave packet and momentum spread narrowing/widening inversely
  • ● Live numeric readouts of \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta p\), and \(\Delta v\)
How to Use
  1. Drag the \(\Delta x\) slider and watch the position curve narrow while the momentum curve widens
  2. Switch the particle dropdown between electron and proton to compare \(\Delta v_{min}\)
  3. Read the numeric panel to see the exact computed uncertainties
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Apply (L2-L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Interpret, Calculate

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Apply \(\Delta x\,\Delta p \geq \hbar/2\) to compute a minimum momentum uncertainty
  • ✓ Interpret the inverse relationship between position and momentum uncertainty visually
  • ✓ Explain why lighter particles (electrons) show larger velocity uncertainty than heavier ones (protons) for the same confinement
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the boxed Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict what happens to \(\Delta p\) if \(\Delta x\) is cut in half
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Set \(\Delta x\) to 0.1 nm (roughly atomic scale) and record \(\Delta p\) and \(\Delta v\) for the electron
  2. Switch to the proton at the same \(\Delta x\) and compare \(\Delta v\)
  3. Drag \(\Delta x\) to its smallest value and observe both curves at their most extreme widths
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Discuss why this is a fundamental property of nature, not a limitation of measurement instruments
  • ● Connect this to why confined electrons in a particle-in-a-box have nonzero minimum kinetic energy
References
  • ● Uncertainty Principle — Wikipedia
  • ● Wave Packet — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations — this textbook

docs.title: Kronig-Penney Band Formation Explorer
docs.text:
Kronig-Penney Band Formation Explorer

← Back to Chapter 5: Quantum Mechanics of Periodic Crystals

Description

This MicroSim has two linked views of the same underlying Kronig-Penney transcendental equation, \(P\sin(\alpha a)/(\alpha a)+\cos(\alpha a)=\cos(ka)\). The Transcendental Equation view plots the left-hand side directly against \(x=\alpha a\) (proportional to \(\sqrt{E}\)), shading in red every region where the curve exceeds \(\pm1\) — these shaded regions are exactly the forbidden band gaps, since no real Bloch wavevector \(k\) can produce a cosine outside that range. The E-k Diagram view inverts the same equation (using \(\arccos\), with no iterative root-finding required) to plot the resulting allowed energy bands directly against \(k\), with Brillouin zone boundaries marked as dashed vertical lines, making visible the chapter's central result: band gaps open exactly at those boundaries.

Key Features

  • ● Two linked views of the same equation: raw transcendental plot and E-k band diagram
  • ● Live-shaded forbidden regions wherever \(|{\rm LHS}|>1\)
  • ● Adjustable barrier strength P spanning the free-electron limit (P=0) to strongly gapped bands
  • ● Brillouin zone boundaries marked in both views for direct visual correlation
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window
How to Use
  1. Drag P to 0 in "Transcendental Equation" view and confirm all shading disappears
  2. Increase P and watch the forbidden (shaded) regions widen around each zone boundary
  3. Switch to "E-k Diagram" and confirm the band-curve gaps line up with the same zone boundaries
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Analyze (L2-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Interpret, Predict, Analyze

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Interpret the Kronig-Penney transcendental equation and identify forbidden energy regions directly from its plot
  • ✓ Predict how increasing barrier strength affects band gap width
  • ✓ Analyze an E-k band diagram to locate band gaps relative to Brillouin zone boundaries
References
  • ● Kronig-Penney Model — Wikipedia
  • ● Bloch's Theorem — Wikipedia
  • ● Electronic Band Structure — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 5: Quantum Mechanics of Periodic Crystals — this textbook

docs.title: Maxwell-Boltzmann Speed Distribution
docs.text:
Maxwell-Boltzmann Speed Distribution

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim plots the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution for a representative gas particle (mass close to an N\(_2\) molecule) as a function of temperature. Dragging the temperature slider shows the curve broaden and its peak shift to higher speed, while numeric readouts show the most probable speed, the RMS speed, and the average kinetic energy \(\langle KE\rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT\) in both joules and electron-volts.

Key Features

  • ● Live-updating curve recomputed on every slider change, from 100 K to 1000 K
  • ● Most-probable-speed and RMS-speed markers shown as labeled dashed vertical lines
  • ● Two one-click presets: Room Temperature (300 K) and Liquid Nitrogen (77 K)
  • ● Numeric readout of average kinetic energy in both joules and electron-volts
How to Use
  1. Drag the temperature slider from 100 K to 1000 K and watch the curve broaden and shift right
  2. Click the two preset buttons to directly compare a cryogenic and a room-temperature condition
  3. Read the numeric panel to see how much the average kinetic energy changes between presets
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand (L2)  |  Bloom Verb: Interpret

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Interpret how raising temperature reshapes the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution
  • ✓ Connect the visual broadening of the curve to the increase in \(\langle KE\rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT\)
  • ✓ Explain why cooling a device changes the thermal energy available to its carriers
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the kinetic theory of gases and the Boltzmann constant from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict how the curve will change if temperature doubles
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Click Liquid Nitrogen (77 K) and note the narrow, left-shifted curve
  2. Click Room Temperature (300 K) and compare the broader, right-shifted curve
  3. Slide up to 1000 K and observe how far the most-probable-speed line moves
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Connect back to Worked Example 12 in the chapter
  • ● Preview that this same statistical reasoning reappears for electrons in Chapters 9–10
References
  • ● Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 1: Kinetic Theory, the Boltzmann Constant, and Thermal Equilibrium — this textbook

docs.title: Miller Indices Explorer
docs.text:
Miller Indices Explorer

← Back to Chapter 3: Crystal Lattices and Structures

Description

This MicroSim lets students set integer Miller indices \((h\,k\,l)\) with three sliders and immediately see the corresponding crystal plane shaded and outlined inside a rotatable wireframe unit cell. The plane is computed from the intercept-form equation \(hX+kY+lZ=1\) (in fractional coordinates of the lattice constant \(a\)) and clipped against the cube boundary, so an index of 0 correctly produces a plane parallel to that axis, and negative indices correctly show whether the plane crosses the displayed unit cell at all.

Key Features

  • ● Three integer sliders for h, k, and l, ranging from −3 to 3
  • ● Preset buttons for the common planes (100), (110), (111), and (200)
  • ● Free 3D rotation via p5.js \(\texttt{orbitControl()}\) — click-drag to spin, scroll to zoom
  • ● Live readout panel showing intercepts and a clear message when the plane misses the displayed cell
How to Use
  1. Drag the h, k, l sliders or click a preset button to choose Miller indices
  2. Click and drag anywhere on the 3D view to rotate the cell and inspect the plane's orientation
  3. Scroll or pinch to zoom in and out
  4. Read the panel below the canvas for the current intercepts and Miller notation
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Compute, Construct

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Compute a plane's axis intercepts from its Miller indices and vice versa
  • ✓ Construct and visually verify the (100), (110), (111), and (200) planes inside a unit cell
  • ✓ Explain why an index of 0 means the plane runs parallel to that axis
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the definition of a crystal plane and the intercept-reciprocal procedure for finding Miller indices
  • ● Ask students to sketch what they expect the (110) plane to look like before opening the MicroSim
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Click through all four presets in order and describe how the shaded polygon's shape changes
  2. Set one index to 0 and confirm the plane becomes parallel to that axis, extending to the cell boundary
  3. Try a negative index and observe the readout panel's message when the plane no longer crosses the displayed cell
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Have students compute the Miller indices for a plane with given intercepts by hand and verify with the sliders
  • ● Discuss how Miller planes like (111) relate to the tetrahedral bonding directions seen in the diamond cubic MicroSim
References
  • ● Miller Index — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 3: Crystal Lattices and Structures — this textbook

docs.title: Particle in a Box Explorer
docs.text:
Particle in a Box Explorer

← Back to Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations

Description

This MicroSim lets students adjust the box width \(L\) (0.1 nm to 5 nm) and quantum number \(n\) (1 to 6) of an electron confined to an infinite square well, plotting the wavefunction \(\psi_n(x) = \sqrt{2/L}\sin(n\pi x/L)\) and the probability density \(|\psi_n(x)|^2\). A side-panel energy-level ladder computed from \(E_n = n^2h^2/(8m_eL^2)\) shows that energy levels are not evenly spaced — they scale as \(n^2\).

Key Features

  • ● Box width slider from 0.1 nm to 5 nm
  • ● Integer quantum-number slider for n = 1 through 6, extended down through n = 0 and to n = -6 for exploration
  • ● Overlaid ψₙ(x) and |ψₙ(x)|² plots with internal nodes marked
  • ● Energy-level ladder diagram for E₁ through E₆, with the selected level highlighted
How to Use
  1. Drag the n slider and count how the number of internal nodes changes
  2. Drag the L slider and watch every level in the energy ladder shift
  3. Compare the highlighted level to the other five to see the n² spacing pattern
  4. Drag n below 1 to see why n = 0 and negative n are excluded from (or redundant with) the physical spectrum
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply / Analyze (L3-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate, Distinguish

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Apply \(\psi_n(x)=\sqrt{2/L}\sin(n\pi x/L)\) to sketch stationary states of a confined particle
  • ✓ Analyze how \(E_n \propto n^2/L^2\) produces unevenly spaced energy levels
  • ✓ Distinguish the wavefunction from the probability density it produces
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the boxed particle-in-a-box wavefunction and energy formulas from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict how many nodes ψ₄ will have before checking
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Step n from 1 to 6 at fixed L and record each internal node count
  2. Fix n = 2 and shrink L from 5 nm to 0.1 nm, noting how quickly E₂ rises
  3. Compare the E₁-E₂ gap to the E₅-E₆ gap in the ladder diagram
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Drag n to 0 live and discuss why it is not a valid state (it would mean no particle at all); drag to a negative n and discuss why it duplicates its positive counterpart rather than describing a new state
  • ● Preview how this quantized-level structure foreshadows the energy bands built from many confined electrons later in the course
References
  • ● Particle in a Box — Wikipedia
  • ● Wave Function — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations — this textbook

docs.title: Photon Energy Across the Electromagnetic Spectrum
docs.text:
Photon Energy Across the Electromagnetic Spectrum

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This chart plots photon energy \(E=hc/\lambda\) against wavelength on logarithmic axes spanning gamma rays to radio waves. The visible-light band (380–700 nm) is shaded, and a dashed reference line marks silicon's 1.12 eV band gap, with a marker showing exactly where that energy falls on the curve (near-infrared, about 1107 nm).

Key Features

  • ● Log-log curve computed directly from \(E=hc/\lambda\) across 12 orders of magnitude in wavelength
  • ● Labeled spectrum bands: gamma ray, X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, and radio
  • ● Shaded visible-light region and a dashed silicon band-gap reference line
  • ● Hover tooltips showing the exact energy and wavelength at any point on the curve
How to Use
  1. Hover over the curve anywhere to read the exact photon energy and wavelength
  2. Find the shaded visible band and note how narrow it is compared to the full spectrum
  3. Locate the red dot where the silicon band-gap line crosses the curve, just past visible light in the near-infrared
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Analyze (L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Compare

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Compare photon energies across the electromagnetic spectrum
  • ✓ Locate where silicon's band gap falls relative to visible light
  • ✓ Explain why a semiconductor absorbs some wavelengths of light but not others
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the photon energy equation \(E=hc/\lambda\) from the chapter
  • ● Ask students whether higher or lower wavelength means higher photon energy
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Hover over the gamma-ray and radio-wave ends of the curve and compare the energy values
  2. Find the visible-light band and read off the energy range of visible photons
  3. Locate the silicon band-gap marker and discuss why light just past red (near-infrared) can still be absorbed
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Connect back to Worked Example 11 in the chapter
  • ● Preview optical absorption and solar cells in Chapter 17
References
  • ● Photon Energy — Wikipedia
  • ● Electromagnetic Spectrum — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 1: Photon Energy — this textbook

docs.title: Quantum Tunneling Probability Explorer
docs.text:
Quantum Tunneling Probability Explorer

← Back to Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations

Description

This MicroSim lets students adjust a rectangular barrier's height ratio \(V_0/E\) (1.1 to 5) and width \(L\) (0.1 nm to 2 nm) for an electron with fixed energy \(E=1\) eV, and see the simplified tunneling approximation \(T \approx e^{-2\kappa L}\), \(\kappa = \sqrt{2m_e(V_0-E)}/\hbar\) update live. A schematic wavefunction shows an oscillating incident/reflected wave, an exponentially decaying curve inside the barrier, and a reduced-amplitude transmitted wave beyond it.

Key Features

  • ● Barrier height ratio slider (V₀/E from 1.1 to 5) with fixed particle energy E = 1 eV
  • ● Barrier width slider from 0.1 nm to 2 nm
  • ● Schematic wavefunction: oscillating (incident+reflected) — decaying (barrier) — oscillating (transmitted)
  • ● Live transmission-probability readout and gauge bar (√T-scaled so tiny probabilities remain visible)
How to Use
  1. Drag the V₀/E slider and watch the decay curve inside the barrier steepen as the barrier gets relatively taller
  2. Drag the barrier width slider and watch T fall rapidly as the barrier widens
  3. Read the numeric T value and gauge bar to judge the transmission probability
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply / Understand (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Calculate, Interpret

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Apply \(T \approx e^{-2\kappa L}\) to estimate tunneling probability through a rectangular barrier
  • ✓ Interpret why T falls off exponentially with both barrier width and height
  • ✓ Recognize the limits of the simplified approximation (valid when \(\kappa L \gg 1\))
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the boxed tunneling approximation and the classically-forbidden-region argument from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict whether doubling barrier width or doubling (V0/E − 1) will hurt transmission more
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Set V₀/E = 1.1 and L = 0.1 nm and record T (should be a large fraction)
  2. Increase L to 2 nm at the same V₀/E and compare
  3. Reset L to 0.1 nm and raise V₀/E to 5, comparing the new T to the very first reading
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Discuss real-world tunneling devices (tunnel diodes, scanning tunneling microscopes, flash memory)
  • ● Preview how tunneling reappears later in the course when discussing thin oxide layers in MOS junctions
References
  • ● Quantum Tunneling — Wikipedia
  • ● Rectangular Potential Barrier — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations — this textbook

docs.title: Reciprocal Lattice and Brillouin Zone Explorer
docs.text:
Reciprocal Lattice and Brillouin Zone Explorer

← Back to Chapter 5: Quantum Mechanics of Periodic Crystals

Description

This MicroSim has two linked views. The Real vs. Reciprocal Lattice view renders a real-space 2D lattice side by side with its reciprocal lattice, with independently adjustable lattice constants a_x and a_y, making the inverse relationship between real-space spacing and reciprocal-space spacing (\(2\pi/a\)) directly visible. The Brillouin Zone view constructs the first Brillouin zone from the reciprocal lattice using the Wigner-Seitz procedure — drawing the perpendicular bisector lines to the nearest reciprocal lattice points and shading the enclosed region, the k-space primitive cell whose boundary is exactly where Chapter 5's Kronig-Penney band gaps open.

Key Features

  • ● Two linked views: Real vs. Reciprocal Lattice, and Brillouin Zone construction
  • ● Independently adjustable a_x, a_y sliders demonstrate the inverse relationship along each axis separately
  • ● Live Wigner-Seitz construction with dashed perpendicular-bisector lines and a shaded first Brillouin zone
  • ● Responsive canvas that resizes with the browser window
How to Use
  1. In "Real vs. Reciprocal Lattice" view, drag a_x and observe the inverse change in reciprocal spacing
  2. Uncheck "Square lattice" and stretch a_x independently of a_y
  3. Switch to "Brillouin Zone" view and watch the shaded zone resize and change proportions to match
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Apply (L2-L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Compare, Construct, Predict

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Compute reciprocal lattice spacing from a real-space lattice constant
  • ✓ Predict how an anisotropic real-space lattice affects the reciprocal lattice and Brillouin zone shape
  • ✓ Construct the first Brillouin zone from a reciprocal lattice using the Wigner-Seitz procedure
References
  • ● Reciprocal Lattice — Wikipedia
  • ● Brillouin Zone — Wikipedia
  • ● Wigner-Seitz Cell — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 5: Quantum Mechanics of Periodic Crystals — this textbook

docs.title: Schrödinger Wavefunction & Eigenstates Visualizer
docs.text:
Schrödinger Wavefunction & Eigenstates Visualizer

← Back to Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations

Description

This MicroSim animates a complex wavefunction \(\psi(x,t)\), plotting its real part, imaginary part, and probability density \(|\psi|^2\) together. In Eigenstate mode it renders a single plane wave \(\psi=Ae^{i(kx-\omega t)}\) — the probability density stays perfectly flat and unchanging while only the complex phase rotates, the defining property of a stationary state. In Wave Packet mode it sums seven plane waves with Gaussian weights and the free-particle dispersion relation \(\omega\propto k^2\) — the components dephase over time, so the probability density localizes into a hump that visibly drifts and spreads.

Key Features

  • ● Start/Stop animation of ψ(x,t) with a dedicated stacked panel for Re[ψ]/Im[ψ] and |ψ|²
  • ● Eigenstate / Wave Packet mode toggle contrasting a flat, time-independent density against a localized, evolving one
  • ● Central k₀ and packet-width Δk sliders reshaping the wave packet's initial localization and spreading rate
  • ● Adjustable animation speed, using an explicitly illustrative "phase-time," not real seconds
How to Use
  1. Start in Eigenstate mode and press Start to see the flat, unchanging probability density
  2. Check "Wave packet" and press Start to see the density localize, drift, and spread
  3. Adjust Δk and compare the initial packet width and how quickly it spreads afterward
  4. Adjust k₀ and observe how the spatial wavelength and phase speed change
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Analyze (L2-L4)  |  Bloom Verb: Visualize, Contrast, Explain

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Distinguish the complex wavefunction ψ from the real, measurable probability density |ψ|²
  • ✓ Explain why a single eigenstate is called a "stationary state" despite its visibly rotating phase
  • ✓ Connect wave-packet spreading to the Heisenberg uncertainty tradeoff between Δk (momentum spread) and initial Δx (position spread)
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the Born interpretation of |ψ|² and the complex nature of ψ from the chapter text
  • ● Ask students to predict whether a "stationary state" means the wavefunction itself is frozen in time
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Run Eigenstate mode and confirm the density panel never changes shape
  2. Switch to Wave Packet mode and let it run 20-30 seconds, noting both the drift and the widening of the hump
  3. Set Δk to its minimum and maximum in turn, comparing the initial packet width in each case
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Discuss why the animation uses illustrative "phase-time" rather than real femtoseconds
  • ● Preview how the very next section, Particle in a Box, produces eigenstates with *shape* by adding boundary conditions that this free-particle model lacks
References
  • ● Wave Function — Wikipedia
  • ● Wave Packet — Wikipedia
  • ● Stationary State — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations — this textbook

docs.title: Unit Cell Repetition Explorer
docs.text:
Unit Cell Repetition Explorer

← Back to Chapter 3: Crystal Lattices and Structures

Description

This MicroSim makes the lattice/unit-cell relationship concrete by literally repeating a single conventional unit cell — Simple Cubic, Body-Centered Cubic, or Face-Centered Cubic — into an N×N×N block, for N from 1 to 4. Every cell in the block uses the exact same atom-position pattern, translated by whole multiples of the lattice constant \(a\) along each axis. Unlike the Crystal Structure Explorer, which shows one cell in full structural detail, this tool's only job is showing what "repeating the unit cell" actually looks like in three dimensions — including an optional cell-by-cell reveal animation that grows the block outward from its center.

Key Features

  • ● N×N×N tiling (N=1 to 4) of SC, BCC, or FCC unit cells by simple translation
  • ● Start/Stop reveal animation that grows the block outward from its center, one cell at a time
  • ● Per-cell vs. outer-boundary wireframe toggle and a camera that automatically reframes as N changes
  • ● Free 3D orbit and zoom, matching the Crystal Structure Explorer's controls
How to Use
  1. Start at N=1 and note the single cell's atom pattern
  2. Increase N to 4 and confirm the exact same pattern has simply repeated
  3. Press Start to watch the block grow outward from its center, cell by cell
  4. Switch structures at the same N and compare atom density between SC, BCC, and FCC
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand (L2)  |  Bloom Verb: Visualize, Describe

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Describe a crystal lattice as a single unit cell repeated by translation in three dimensions
  • ✓ Relate the lattice constant a to the overall size of an N-cell block (N·a per side)
  • ✓ Visually compare atom density across SC, BCC, and FCC at the same lattice constant
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the lattice, basis, and unit cell definitions from the chapter's introduction
  • ● Ask students to sketch, on paper, what they expect a 2×2×2 block of cubes to look like before seeing it rendered
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Step N from 1 to 4 for Simple Cubic and confirm the cell count matches N³ each time
  2. Press Start at N=4 and watch the outward-growing reveal animation
  3. Switch to FCC at the same N and compare the visual atom density to SC
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Discuss why real crystals (billions of unit cells) can be fully described by specifying just one cell plus its repetition rule
  • ● Preview the Crystal Structure Explorer for a detailed look at each structure's specific atom positions, coordination number, and packing factor
References
  • ● Bravais Lattice — Wikipedia
  • ● Crystal Structure — Wikipedia
  • ● Crystal Structure Explorer — this textbook, for structure-specific detail
  • ● Chapter 3: Crystal Lattices and Structures — this textbook

docs.title: Vector Components and Addition
docs.text:
Vector Components and Addition

← Back to Chapter 1: Physics and Math Foundations

Description

This MicroSim lets students build two vectors, \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\), by setting their magnitude and direction angle, and see the resulting x and y components. A tip-to-tail construction shows how the two vectors add to form the resultant \(\vec{R}=\vec{A}+\vec{B}\), with all magnitudes, angles, and components displayed numerically.

Key Features

  • ● Four sliders controlling the magnitude and angle of two independent vectors
  • ● Dashed component projections onto the x and y axes (toggle on/off)
  • ● Tip-to-tail construction showing \(\vec{B}\) redrawn from the tip of \(\vec{A}\) to form the resultant
  • ● Full numeric readout of magnitude, angle, and components for A, B, and R
How to Use
  1. Adjust |A| and θA to change the blue vector's magnitude and direction
  2. Adjust |B| and θB to change the green vector
  3. Watch the red resultant \(\vec{R}\) update as you move either vector
  4. Toggle component projections to see how \(A_x\), \(A_y\) relate to \(|\vec{A}|\) and \(\theta_A\)
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Apply (L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Construct, compute

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Decompose a vector into its x and y components given a magnitude and angle
  • ✓ Add two vectors component-wise and graphically using the tip-to-tail method
  • ✓ Recover the magnitude and direction of a resultant vector from its components
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the definition of a vector versus a scalar from the chapter
  • ● Ask students to predict the components of a vector at 90° and at 180°
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Set A to magnitude 5 at 0° and read off its components
  2. Set A to magnitude 5 at 90° and compare
  3. Add a second vector B and verify \(R_x = A_x+B_x\) and \(R_y=A_y+B_y\) against the on-screen readout
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Connect back to the Vectors subsection in the Vector Calculus section of the chapter
  • ● Preview that force and electric field are vectors added the same way

docs.title: Wave-Particle Duality Explorer
docs.text:
Wave-Particle Duality Explorer

← Back to Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations

Description

This MicroSim fires individual particles, one at a time, at a barrier with one or two slits and a detector screen beyond it. Each particle's landing position is sampled from the Fraunhofer interference intensity distribution, so any single detection looks random, but the accumulated pattern of many detections reveals interference fringes when both slits are open — and a single smooth band when only one slit is open. This is the classic demonstration that quantum particles are always detected individually (particle behavior) while the statistics of many detections follow a wave-interference pattern (wave behavior).

Key Features

  • ● Start/Stop animation firing one particle at a time — the project's first animated MicroSim
  • ● One-slit / two-slit toggle to directly contrast diffraction alone against interference
  • ● Slit separation and wavelength sliders that reshape the fringe spacing live
  • ● Persistent accumulated pattern that survives across many particles, plus a Clear Pattern reset
  • ● Live readouts for particle count and predicted fringe spacing, plus a reference intensity curve
How to Use
  1. Press Start with two slits open and watch particles land one at a time
  2. Let 100+ particles accumulate until fringe bands are clearly visible
  3. Clear the pattern and switch to one slit to see the fringes disappear
  4. Adjust the d and λ sliders and observe the fringe spacing readout and reference curve change
Learning Objectives

Bloom Level: Understand / Apply (L2-L3)  |  Bloom Verb: Observe, Predict, Explain

After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • ✓ Describe wave-particle duality as individually-localized detections that collectively follow a wave-interference pattern
  • ✓ Predict how fringe spacing changes with slit separation and wavelength
  • ✓ Explain why closing one slit removes the interference fringes but not the particle detections
Lesson Plan Before the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Review the Davisson-Germer experiment and photon/electron duality from the chapter text
  • ● Ask students to predict what a screen would show if particles behaved purely as tiny bullets passing through one slit or the other
During the Simulation (10 minutes)
  1. Start with two slits open and watch the first 10-20 particles — note how scattered/unpredictable individual hits look
  2. Let the pattern build past 100 particles and identify the bright and dark fringe bands
  3. Clear the pattern, switch to one slit, rebuild it, and compare the two final patterns side by side (screenshot or sketch both)
After the Simulation (5 minutes)
  • ● Discuss why "which slit did it go through?" is not answerable without destroying the interference pattern (mention, at a conceptual level, that measuring the path removes the fringes)
  • ● Preview how this same duality underlies the de Broglie wavelength and Heisenberg uncertainty relations covered next in the chapter
References
  • ● Wave-Particle Duality — Wikipedia
  • ● Double-Slit Experiment — Wikipedia
  • ● Davisson-Germer Experiment — Wikipedia
  • ● Chapter 2: Quantum Mechanics Foundations — this textbook
